Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I want to call attention to a certain misrepresentation which appears in what purports to be a letter issued by the Railway Department to its employees. I am quoting from the ' Daily Telegraph ' of St. John, New Brunswick, Saturday, June 6:
Intercolonial Railway employees here have been notified by a circular, a copy of which is posted in the freight shed, that salaries or wages will not likely be paid until further supplies have been voted by parliament.
The circular which bears the name of the late superintendent G. M. Jarvis and is dated from Truro on June 3, informs all concerned

that a letter dated June 2, had been received from the general manager which reads as follows:
I am instructed to advise you that the interim partial appropriation voted by parliament for works and. staff under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals, will shortly be exhausted, if not already so, and that no further appropriation has been obtained from parliament at the present date, and to instruct you to notify the several members of your staff of the position, leaving it to their option to decide whether they will continue work on the understanding that no salary or wages will be paid them until further supplies have been voted.
Similar notices are posted at Moncton and elsewhere along the line. A Moncton despatch says: In view of the circular, employees are wondering whether or not they are to receive any pay this month. The office employees, including men in the shippings, train men, &c., have yet to be paid.
What I complain of Is that those instructions, issued from the Department of Railways and Canals

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What date ?

It must have been previous to June 2, because on June 2 the General Manager sent his circular to the different road superintendents. Therefore the instructions must have gone from him before June 1 in order to have enabled him to issue these instructions on June 2. The idea no doubt was to make the people working on the Intercolonial Railway believe that the opposition were preventing them from getting their pay. As a matter of fact, however, the Minister of Railways has never asked this parliament for Supply to pay the employees of the Intercolonial Railway or on the canals. Last Friday night, after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) had moved that the committee rise and report progress, and after midnight when we had been sitting from 11 in the morning, the Minister of Railways- evidently by preconcerted arrangement- rose and said he would like to get some Supply. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) objected that it was very late and that some of the members of the committee in connection with railways and canals, on the opposition side, were not present. The minister demurred to this on the ground that he could not be here on Monday. Well, we know why the minister could not be here on Monday. The minister is not detained by anything in connection with his department from being here; the minister is up in Brockville attending to the provincial elections. The minister has a right, if he sees fit, to take part in the provincial elections, I have no fault to find with that at all. But the minist<>r should not neglect the work of his department in order to take part in provincial elections. We are now going into Supply; if the Minister of Railways were here 318
there would be no difficulty in getting Supply for the employees of his department. But as I say, he has never asked for Supply except in the manner I have mentioned, on Friday night. I say that this instruction that has been issued from the Department of Railways and Canals is absolutely and entirely misleading, and is a misrepresentation of the true situation here. We have been charged with obstruction; and my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., (Mi', Carvel]) stated the other day that a great many resolutions had been moved by the opposition, who had taken up a great deal of time unnecessarily. Now as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the greater portion of the time of this House, as will be found by an examination of ' Hansard,' has been taken up by lion, gentlemen opposite.
Oh.

My hon. friend says oh. I have carefully examined the ' Hansard ' from the first of this session in November down to the end of January, and during that time hon. gentlemen opposite have taken up a considerably larger portion of the time.
Do you include in that the time you devoted in asking questions over Supply?

The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) has asked a question, I do not know what-he means by that. I have taken very little time in asking questions over Supply; in fact I do not think, if there is any person that can be accused of obstruction on either side of the House, that any one can properly accuse me of having unnecessarily taken up the time of this House. I have taken up very little time, less time than my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell); but the short time I have taken up has been far more effective, so far as the general business of the country was concerned,, than the much longer time taken up by the member for Carleton, because no man can use more words and say less than that hon. gentleman. Now I have examined the discussion of the various resolutions that were debated, the resolutions which the hon. member for Carleton said were silly and absurd. If they were silly and absurd, it is a singular thing that the ministerial members should find it necessary to talk so much about them. Of course my hon. friend, when he made that remark, did not mean it, he only made it for the purpose of getting a laugh from his friends. I find that on the various resolutions that were introduced in this House and discussed from the time we began to sit in November down to January, the ministerial members occupied thirty-eight columns of ' Hansard ' more than the opposition members did -discussing these various resolutions which



the hon. member for Carleton said were silly and ridiculous.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What was the number in each case, the totals for each side?

I can give them in detail, I can show the Minister of Finance how much time he wasted. Now take some of the larger questions. I find that on the address, the Prime Minister used up twenty-five columns of ' Hansard I find that the Minister of Finance used thirty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on the address.

Yes, he was the worst offender on the address. Now on the address the opposition used up more columns of the ' Hansard ' than did the government, the government spoke 176 columns, while the opposition spoke 275. But in the debate on the immigration question, the Postmaster General was the worst offender, for he spoke 28 columns. The Minister of the Interior, in that debate, spoke 17 columns; total, 54 columns to the government and only 24 to the opposition, a debit of 30 against the government. Then on the motion for the appointment of a fishery commissioner introduced by the hon. mem-/ ber for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), the government spoke 27 columns to the opposition 12, making 15 against the government. On the British Columbia legislation, the government spoke 22 columns to the opposition one. On the original documents discussion, the opposition spoke 35 columns and the government 11. On the Franco-Can-adian trade treaty, the government spoke) 63 columns and the opposition 44, nineteen against the government. On the seed grain question, the government spoke 22 columns to the opposition 13. On the constitution of the Senate, the government spoke 53 columns to the opposition 50. On the motion of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Air. Ralph Smith) on oriental immigration, the government spoke 57 columns and the opposition none; that debate was confined entirely to the members from British Columbia. On the motion of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Air. Alonk) respecting the FrancojCanadian trade treaty, the opposition spoke ten columns and the government one. Concerning original documents there were two debates; in the one on the motion of the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), the opposition spoke 41 and the government 22. On all these different resolutions there is a total against the government of 38 columns of ' Hansard,' and yet we are charged with obstruction. Now what is true of that time is also true of the balance of the time, and even in greater measure. It is natural that the opposition should occupy more time than the government. because we are here to criticise, to ask questions with respect to these various matters. But in these cases the government apparently desired that Supply should Air. FOWLER.
not pass,_ there can be no other conclusion. The ministers in giving their explanations, have given them very fully, in many cases more fully perhaps than was absolutely necessary, and in this way time has been wasted. But what I object to, Air. Speaker, is misrepresentation on the part of the responsible minister of a department, when that minister knows very well that he has never asked for any appropriation from this House to pay the employees in his department.

speechtext: In regard to the number of columns of ' Hansard ' that might be occupied by the respective parties, I have not taken the trouble to make any analysis, but I would suggest to the hon. gentleman that if he wished to go further into the question be should reduce the whole time to the basis of so much per column for th'e average member, and he will discover that inasmuch as our numbers are two to one, roughly speaking, as compared with hon. gentlemen opposite, I have no doubt he will find that the proportion of time occupied by the average member of the opposition is vastly greater than the proportion of time occupied by the average member on the government side of the House.
That means nothing.

I desire to say a word or two on

the question of obstruction. The hon gentleman (Mr. Fielding) who has just spoken said it is not a question of the measure of time occupied, and that, 1 think, is true to a large extent, for surely any person who considers the matter at ail carefully will realize that the opposition must necessarily occupy more time, if they are to adequately discharge their duty, than is occupied by the government and their supporters. I entirely dissent from the suggestion that in this matter we are to be measured by numbers. If there were only ten men in opposition here, the duty would rest upon them, with even greater responsibility, perhaps, than if there were a hundred. The opposition, whether few or many are bound to reasonably scrutinize and criticise the propositions advanced by the government from time to time, and it is altogether immaterial whether this work is done by many or by few, and it is really immaterial how much time is occupied, so that the time is usefully employed. I, for one, will not hesitate at any time to take up whatever time may seem necessary to discuss any question that may arise in order that I may fairly place my views before that House or the committee as the case may be. I may say, in passing, that from a hasty and somewhat incomplete analysis of the proceedings of this House during the last six months,
I am led to the conclusion that the government have, as a matter of fact, occupied quite as much time as have the opposition. But that is not so material to my mind, as the fact which forces itself upon attention, that, on very many occasions, the government have manifestly put up their supporters for the purpose of marking time, for the reason, evidently, that they had not ready the legislation necessary to bring before the House. It requires no elaborate research to discover that this government, this session, have been notably remiss in bringing down legislation, and that the long time to which this session has been drawn out is attributable mainly to the fact that the government have not put themselves in a position to supply the House with the matters which have to be dealt with before we can prorogue. However I more particularly desire to call your attention to a statement made and repeated in this House in somewhat varied form- insultingly repeated, I may say-by some distinguished members of this House (not always by members of the government), to the effect that the opposition have been delaying the progress of the House and blocking the Supply by the introduction of ridiculous resolutions supported by ridiculous arguments. I cook the trouble to look over the month of April to see how the oratory was apportioned during that month, as between this side and that. I find that the government members took up 436 columns and the opposition 326*, showing a surplus of 109J columns of Liberal oratory over Tory oratory. I find there were two main resolutions introduced-one relating to the Hudson Bay Railway, which was submitted by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles), and which took up some little time; the other, proposed by my hon. friend from Jacques' Cartier (Mr. Monk), related to the cessation of immigration [DOT] bounties. In addition to the discussion on these two main resolutions, there was a short debate on the postal mail service introduced by the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), and then we bad the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. Lavergne), during one afternoon, moving the adjournment of the House. The hon. member for St. Hya-cintbe (Mr. Beauparlant) had quite a good deal to say with regard to the criminal code

amendments. Therefore, as regards the month of April at all events-the only month I have looked over-I find that the opposition cannot be accused of having taken up more time than the government side. As a matter of fact, they took up 1094 columns less. Then as regards the moving of resolutions, one was introduced by a member supporting the government and the other by a member on this side.

I wish merely to make one or two remarks. In the first place, I have listened with a good deal of interest to the tabulation of the resolutions submitted this session by members of the opposition. I am very glad that they were massed together so that the country may see practically the effective answers to the wild statements made in the newspaper press and sometimes in this House, namely, that the resolutions proposed by the opposition were merely theoretical and designed to waste time. I do not think you can say of any one of those resolutions that it was purely academic. I do not think you can come to any other conclusion than they had the practical object of drawing attention to abuses and proposing a remedy. I am willing to let those resolutions go to the public, and I think no parliament need be ashamed of the discussion we have had on them.
It has evidently become solely the duty of the opposition to criticise the acts and policies of the government. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if we had to depend on gentlemen who support the government to raise a single voice of criticism or dissent along any one of the lines traced in these resolutions, would we have had one of them presented to this House? It does not seem to be considered the function of supporters of the government to raise a single note of protest or criticism regarding either any measure of the government or the estimates. That has to be done by the opposition, and the opposition are here for that purpose. No opposition would be worth its salt if it did not carry out that purpose, and no country would long tolerate an opposition which failed to do its duty in that respect.
Take the estimates. The government have brought forward $100,000,000 or more. Will any one have the hardihood to deny that if it were not for the members on the opposition side, these estimates would all go through practically without a word of criticism? The supi>orters of the government do not consider that they have any duty in that respect. The Minister of Finance would soon set them in their proper place, according to his idea, if they attempted to criticise the estimates. They are here to do the bidding of the government and not to criticise its acts or policy. Just as in the Public Accounts Committee, there would be no criticism or examination of a single item if it were not for the opposition. I am not sure that it was not
the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who made the astounding suggestion a week ago that he thought the opposition ought to pass the estimates without any criticism.
I hope that the opposition will never be so relax in its duty as to fail to criticise the estimates. When millions of dollars are put before us in block sums, it becomes absolutely necessary to find out what this money is wanted for. A vote comes down for $5,000,000 for the post office. It is divided into three items only, millions in each. And this is only illustrative of many other resolutions brought down in Supply. You might just as well argue in favour of bringing in one resolution providing for the appropriation of $100,000,000 for the government, to be spent by their different departments, and pass it through without criticism as to take up this blind mass estimates of millions of dollars for a given department, nothing definitely shown, either by statement in the estimates or by the explanations of the minister as to what exact use is to be made of the money covered by this lump vote. This, I think, the country will quite understand-that, if we are to have an extravagant government, we must have an over-vigilant opposition, that if we are to have a government with so many bad places in its policy and so many worse places in its administration, then the opposition must take the time to thoroughly criticise-so far as it can against the obstructive tactics of the government in committee and in this House-and bring to the knowledge of the country the facts concerning each vote.

Though the item has stood on the Order Paper for eighteen days, we know no more about the Bill than we did on the 22nd of May last. And there are other government measures not yet before us. We understand that a measure is to be introduced with respect to the Hudson Bay Railway. That has not even been placed upon the Order Paper. Nor have we any means of judging what its terms may be. We were advised in the speech

from the Throne that a measure is to be introduced with regard to the boundaries of Manitoba. But the House, up to the present time, is in complete ignorance what that measure may be. When hon. gentlemen on the other side suggest that the labours of the session should come to an end within five months, it would be well for them to bear in mind that if parliament had ended within that time, each of these three important measures could not have been brought before the House at all. And one, if not two of these measures, was mentioned in the speech from the Throne. It is hardly worth while to look at the matter from one standpoint alone, but we must bear in mind that the most important measures of the session are not yet before the House, nor does the House understand what their terms are to be.

It is quite easy to
see the effort made to-day, to cloud the issue which is now before the House and the country.	The motive is quite
transparent and the reasons also. We have been told on the floor of the House by members high and low on the opposition side that Supply would not be granted, the .business of the House would be blocked, the aims of the government would be blocked, unless the government would drop clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Bill. It is easy to understand that this is the basis and motive of the opposition which we have had to carrying on the business of the country. Perhaps I may be permitted to say that, when we introduced the Election Bill, we received the criticisms made by gentlemen on the other side in no unfriendly spirit, not with any determination to force it down their throats willing or unwilling. We received their criticism, I believe, in a fair spirit, with an idea of improving the Bill, and meeting their criticism as far as we might. With regard to clause 1, the motives which have been attributed to us d0 not exist at all. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated that, as far as Quebec was concerned, the object was to have the votes of the aliens employed on the Transcontinental Railway on the lists. There is no such intention. We are willing.to meet hon. gentlemen on the other side when this Bill is called up and discuss these questions on their merits and endeavour to meet their wishes as far as possible. We are told that section 17 is an attempt to interfere with the secrecy of the ballot.' I have no desire to discuss. the Bill, but I may be permitted to say that the effect of section 17 in the Bill as introduced is simply to provide that the honest elector who casts his vote shall not be disfranchised either by the accidental action of the deputy returning officer or, worse, by the wilful action of such officer.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The Bill does not provide more than that. But it may be that there are reasons why even this mild remedy should not be adopted in the public interest. We are willing to discuss that with our own friends to see whether the law should remain as it is, or whether it should be amended. We are willing to discuss whether it should be left in the power of the deputy returning officer to disfranchise any elector, or any ten or twenty electors, or whether the honest elector who casts his ballot should be responsible only for his own action and not made to suffer for the action of another man. But the question is not upon the Election Bill. The first duty of parliament is to vote Supply-and the question of the Election Bill and all other legislation is set aside. Generally, when parliament discusses legislation, the Supply is voted a year in advance, the machinery of government runs smoothly. But through the change that has taken place in the fiscal year, by which it ends on March 31, instead of June 30, the country has been left without Supply and the business of the government cannot be carried on. We did what is always done under such circumstances-for this has happened before-we applied to the opposition to give us one-quarter of the Supply covered by the resolutions before the House. We were not granted one-quarter, but we were granted one-eiglith, which carried us up to about May 15. On May 15, a similar demand was made, but, up to the present time, it has not been granted. The first duty of the House, at the present time, therefore, is to see to it that the supplies are voted. If the Election Bill does not pass, if the Civil Service Bill does not pass, if the Hudson Bay Bill does not pass, the country still goes on- the public will be inconvenienced, some valuable improvements will be set aside, some valuable reforms will remain to be taken up another year, but the country will still go on. But the country cannot go on unless the creditors of the country are paid, unless the civil servants of the country get their salaries, unless the whole machinery of government is carried on- and this is what we are trying to effect at the present moment. My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says that we want the opposition to swallow these estimates holus bolus. No, we do not want anything of the kind. All legitimate criticism can be made, and ought to be made. But, for the last two or three weeks, what have we obtained from hon. gentlemen opposite ? We have obtained the vote for the Post Office, the vote for the Customs and part of the vote for the Department of the Interior.
And the Mounted Police.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And the Mounted Police, also-certainly, there could be

no criticism over that. These votes have taken two or three weeks' time. It is of no use to tell us that the opposition is facilitating the business. They may or they may not, just as they choose. But I have to point out to them that at the present time the duty of the government and the duty of the opposition is to see that the wheels of government are not clogged, that the King's government is carried on, that the public service is carried on, that the public servants and the creditors of the country are paid the money that is due them. If our friends opposite at the present time will give us what it is their duty to give us, there will be no difficulty whatever.	[DOT]
What does the right hon. gentlemen mean by that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I mean to give us enough Supply to carry on the business of the government.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Let me direct the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that since the 20th of May the voting of Supply has gone on at the rate of about a million dollars a day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: At the rate of a million dollars a day ! And we were told on the floor of the House that if we would withdraw clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Bill the whole Supply would be voted in five minutes. I do not care whether you vote it at the rate of a million a day, or $500,000 a day; what I do care is that every day the government should have enough money at its disposal to carry on, not new projects, but the ordinary purposes which the government have to undertake as a matter of course every year. An hon. gentleman stated some time ago in this House that he was surprised that the government, with so large a majority, could not get Supply. That hon. gentleman surely must understand, and the whole country must understand, that under the rules governing parliamentary procedure, rules which we have adopted from Great Britain and of which we are all proud, every member of parliament has the right to speak and protect himself, the opposition have the right to protect themselves. At the same time, while the rules of parliament give the opposition power to protect themselves, and the right to speak, when the House is in Supply, once, twice, three time, four times, a hundred times, to take up the time of the House for a week, or a month or a year, the only limit which the opposition ought to recognize upon their privilege to speak is their own sense of what is reasonable and fair.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman suggest that during the time I have mentioned, the opposition have unduly criticised ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am surprised at the hon. gentleman's interruption. What else have they been doing?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I venture to say that during the ten days I have mentioned, more time has been taken up by the ministers than by the opposition.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I daresay, because the minister had to answer the questions put to him, not once, but twice, three times, again and again, and again; and after the minister had given his answer and his explanation to one hon. gentleman, the same question was repeated by some other hon. gentleman, and the same answer had to be repeated, and the same explanation given many times over. Under such circumstances we have been forced to speak much more often than we should have been. But I leave it to the common sense of my hon. friends on the other side, What else have they been doing but giving usl Supply in driblets, while the time has been going' on? But we have now come to a point when, not only the government, but the opposition must recognize that it is their duty to see that the business of the country is fairly carried on.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Dominion Lands-chargeable to income-* commissioner's salary, $3,200; salaries of the outside service, $321,800.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why does not the Minister of Railways and Canals go on with his estimates for the Intercolonial ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Minister of Railways and Canals will be prepared to go on with his estimates to-morrow, I hope.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The reason I asked that was because we have been told that the members on this side of the House should be in their places attending to public business. If that is a practical observation as applied to private members, it is much more practical as applied to ministers of the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The ministers are here to-day. But the Minister of the Interior has taken up his estimates which, in the judgment of the government, are important.
We would like to have an explanation of this item.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVER (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
.The sum of $300,000 was voted last session for the fiscal year 1907-8. It was estimated that the sum of $325,000 would be required for the next year, an increase of $25,000. There are 362 employees to be paid out of this appropriation, and to cover their salaries for the twelve months, the sum of $320,760 will be required, leaving a balance of $4,330 to be used for increases to these clerks who will become entitled to

the same during the twelve months ending March 31, 1909.
Who is the commissioner?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. J. W. Greenway.
The minister mentioned that there were $4,000 required for increases in salaries, hut that $325,000 was required. What does he propose to do with the other $20,000?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Since the last vote was submitted to parliament there have been a number of appointments to this service which will take up about $20,000 of the amount, leaving approximately $5,000 which will be available to pay the statutory increases or the increases which will be on all fours with the statutory increases of the inside service.
Mr. FOWLER, Were these appointments rendered necessary by increased work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The work has increased and must necessarily increase from year to year. I had occasion to explain to the House, when the civil government estimates of the Department of the Interior were up, that although th,e number of homestead entries has not increased since last year, the increase in the number which took place three years ago is now bearing fruit in increased work in the department because of the work entailed by the inspection of homesteads, the recommendations for patents, and intermediate to these, the applications for cancellation. The taking of the homestead entry is the smallest part of the work connected with the land transaction. It is when we deal with the entry afterwards that the work accrues. Commencing five years ago, there was a very rapid increase of homestead entries from year to year, the number having risen from 10,000 to 20,000, to 30,000 and finally to 40,000 and it is due to this large increase that the work to-day is increasing in the department.
Mr. FOWLER, Are these additional officers principally homestead inspectors ?
Mr. OLIVER, There are some additional homestead inspectors, but the requirements run through the whole list of the service. The inspection of a homestead is only one feature of the case. There are applications for extensions, for cancellations, for patents ; there is an enormous amount of work that begins at the land office in the west and ends in the office here.
That means more clerical work then ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: More clerical work as well as more outside work, such as the work of inspection.
Are the new clerks who have been taken on principally men or women ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The larger number are men, but there are a number of women.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As I understand it, the expansion of a few years ago is of such a character that it entails a considerable increase in the work ?
Mr. OLIVER, Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is why you are asking for this increase so far as it is not devoted to increases in the salaries of officers ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I call the hon. gentlemen's attention to the curious itemizing of his estimates in this respect ? You have the huge item of salaries ; I do not object to that There could be no object in the itemizing of salaries. Then you have an item of $100,000 for contingencies, the information in regard to which is of a very general character. Then you have protection of timber $100,000; the information in regard to this is also of a very general character, Then you come down to the salary of one carpenter, $914.50. It seems to me to be in curious contrast-huge items of a very general character and then one item for the salary of one special carpenter, $914.50. I do not understand it, although there may be consideration that make these large items necessary in special cases. The minister explained matters in that regard to my satisfaction the other evening. Would it not be possible with respect to an item like this to divide it up a little more without inconvenience to the public service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be possible to divide the salary item up but it would be difficult to divide contingencies so that the item would be intelligible and at the same time applicable to the case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You may desire to have it general in order to have the money available for a purpose that may not be foreseen.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, for things that may not be foreseen. We know that the services will be required but we cannot tell how much will be required for each. As to this unfortunate carpenter's salary, he is not in any of the classifications that are covered by the general vote, and, of course as we are ground between the upper and nether millstone of parliamentary criticism and the Auditor General's check, we have to put his salary into the estimates in this way.
Is he at Banff or at Ottawa ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Ottawa.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems clear that he cannot be regarded as a contingency or he would not be by himself.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
I notice that the vote for the protection of timber comes under this heading. Have you added a number of fire rangers or taken additional precautions for the protection of timber ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have added two forest rangers.
In what districts

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One at Edmonton and another stationed at Sapperton, in the New Westminister district.

I would call the minister's attention to this very important feature ; that is the protection of forests, not only in British Columbia but in the Northwest. I think that the money expended for the purpose of protecting our forests from fire is money well spent, indeed, and I do not think at the present time the precaution taken is sufficient. I do not believe there are enough fire rangers provided in the west and, particularly since this new Grand Trunk Pacific Railway is going through different wooded sections of the country every precaution should be taken as you have the danger from natural causes in addition to the danger from the ' recklessness of the class of men who are employed upon these railways, who are very largely foreigners, who care nothing whatever for the interests of this country and who would be rather delighted iu doing mischief of that kind just for the sake of seeing the flames arise. I think it is most important that the minister should look into that matter very closely and appoint the necessary number of fire rangers.

I would like to ask what the policy of the minister is in regard to the filling of vacancies in the different land offices of the Northwest and in the outside service generally. I asked him a question the other day with regard to filling a vacancy at Edmonton and, from the answer he gave, I understand he brought a man in entirely from the outside, a gentleman who could not possibly have any knowledge of the details of the work and who would have to rely upon the juniors, the men whom he was going to supersede in that event, to coach him and make him familiar with the work that he was going to do. I do not know whether the same policy is being carried on in other parts of the Northwest, but I would imagine that it is an extremely bad thing for the whole outside service to let men labour under the impression that no matter how good their work is, they have no chance of appointment to the best positions going. I would like the minister to give us a general idea of what his policy is in regard to promotion in the outside service.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is very hard to lay down a general policy that would not be chiefly
known, like the rules of English grammar, by its exceptions. In the case mentioned, the appointment was made of a gentleman who had hitherto been outside the service but we believed that by reason of his opportunities he was able to bring into the service ability and advantages that no person whom we then had in the service at that point was able to bring, and we had need of all the men who might be presumed to be of equal standing at other points where they were employed.
I may say generally that while it is very desirable that employees in the land offices shall have accurate knowledge of the routine of the office and of the department generally, in as much as they are from day to day in immediate touch with the people for whose convenience and benefit these offices exist, it is even more necessary that the man at the head of the land office should have such standing and qualification as will be to his advantage in coming in contact with the public at large. We may be able to get men who are perfectly competent to transact clerical work, who can keep in touch with the routine of the office and of the department, who are in themselves in every way creditable persons, but who lack the knowledge of matters and things in the world outside that would enable them to deal satisfactorily with the general public and with the questions between the department and the general public which arise from day to day in those offices and the settlement of which questions is really the main duty of the land agent. Under these circumstances, while we have given due consideration to the possibilities of promotion from within the service, it would not be fair to the House or to the service to let it be understood that the principle of promotion was our leading principle in providing for the outside service. It is absolutely necessary that we should have men in touch with outside conditions and we cannot always depend upon meeting that requirement by promotions from the service. When occasion arises we have to do the best we can and take them from the outside.
At one o'clock, committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

At one o'clock the minister had been giving the reasons for bringing in men from the outside and putting them in good positions in the outside service over the heads of officials who had qualified themselves for those positions. The reasons which he gave were, to my mind, a considerable reflection on all the officials of the outside service. To say that men who are dealing with the public every day with regard to the special questions which come

before their offices, who Are thoroughly conversant with all the difficulties which arise in connection with those dealings, who understand how the ordinary run of questions are ordinarily dealt with, who know what questions can be decided locally and what questions have to be referred to headquarters-to say that these men are not as competent as anybody can be to deal with the usages of a land office is to my mind a reflection upon them. It is all the more of a reflection to say that they are not as competent as men brought in from the outside, with possibly no experience whatever of official life and having to learn all the duties after they come in. This must have an extremely bad effect on the members of the civil service. The Civil Service Commissioners in their report referred to the outside customs officers as men without hope. Unless the minister is careful, that will be the condition of members of the outside service of the Department of the Interior if this course is constantly pursued. Difficulties are inevitable in dealing with the many questions which come before these land officers if you bring in men without official training-men who are placed in those positions probably for services rendered to the party. However, much such men may wish to lay aside all partisan feelings in taking up a position of that sort, it would be impossible for them entirely to divest themselves of party feeling. Many cases have come to my notice in which I have been unable to avoid the feeling that local officials have allowed party bias to influence their judgment in dealing with the cases which came before them. I think that must inevitably be so if you bring in men without proper training for the positions which they are to occupy and who are being promoted for party services. The minister and'his senior officials here may say honestly that they desire to administer the land laws without any bias or party favour, but if they are being served by men who are strong partisans I think they will find it impossible to prevent party bias from creeping into the service. When the minister was speaking of the Edmonton case, he spoke of there being no one on the spot as -well qualified in his opinion as the man he brought in for the position of land agent there. It struck me that the first idea in his mind was that it was necessary to make a promotion of some one who happened to be in the land office at Edmonton. I think that would not be a good thing for the service. Where a man shows himself to have done his work well, it does not matter whether he happens to be in the particular suboffice where the vacancy occurs or not, and it should be possible for the minister to bring in the most efficient man he can find in the outside service to fill the position. Men should be encouraged to do their work well with the hope that if they do it properly Mr. LAKE
they will be entitled to promotion at one time or another. I would like to ask the minister whether within the last couple of years he has brought in any others to take positions in the outside service who have not already been doing work in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In establishing the new office at Moosejaw the gentleman who was appointed agent was from the outside. In the new office at Humboldt the agent appointed was from the outside. In the case of the Lethbridge office we promoted a man from the staff as agent. In the Regina office we also promoted a man from the staff. In each case we acted according to what we thought would give the best results in the public interest.

In these other two cases I presume you had to bring in other officials to help the untrained officials put in as agents. What was the reason for the changes which took place in the Moosejaw office? I understood that another official had been appointed as agent and that after he had been doing his work for a short time the decision came that the office was to be closed, and then a further decision came that it was to be reopened again with the new officer in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend must be misinformed. The gentleman now in the office is the gentleman who was first appointed, and there has been no break in the business such as my hon. friend suggests.

Has the minister any intention of opening the land office at Pin-cher Creek which was closed about a year ago? It is very desirable to have an office there. Our district is thirty miles away from the next subagency and there is a very large settlement extending in every direction. In my opinion there never was sufficient pay to induce a first-class man to keep the place. Would the minister not promise to reopen that office?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reason of the resignation was that the salary paid was not sufficient. The agent was quite an efficient man and did very good work during a number of years. In fact he did so good work and so much of it that there did not remain sufficient to be done to warrant our paying him any increase of salary. A subagency is opened simply as a temporary convenience and does not at all replace the land agency. It is simply to enable people, who are not familiar with clerical work and have some difficulty in putting down upon paper their intentions, to get information from the subagent and deal with a person responsible to the agency. While it is our policy to open these agencies as the press of settlement renders them necessary, it is also our policy to close them when

the need has passed ; and although I would not say that the need has altogether passed at Pincher Creek, yet when the agent saw fit to resign because his salary was not sufficient and when, because of the general settlement of the country, the need for a subagency had decreased, we did not feel called upon to reopen the office.

The minister is aware that the settlers have to travel from Crow's Nest Pass all the way to Fort Macleod at present, which is a great inconvenience. Would the minister be disposed to continue the office at a salary of $25 per month ? Even at that price a suitable man might be found.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If we could get an efficient and reliable man to act as subagent, I think we would be willing to pay him the sum suggested, but of course, as the business Is not as large as it was some years ago, there Is not the same necessity for a subagent. If however we could get one satisfactory to us to do the work at a fair compensation, there would be no objection to reopening the office.
Does this cover the cost of the National Park at Banff ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, there is another item dealing with the park.

With regard to the Moose-jaw case, the statement was made in the papers that Mr. Plaxton had been appointed at Moosejaw, that after having had the office open some little time, the office was closed and the papers were packed up and sent to Regina. But after a week or ten days the boxes were returned from Regina unopened and sent to Mr. Plaxton by mistake. In the meantime another land agent had been appointed. Why was Mr. Plaxton dismissed and a new agent appointed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There was a subagency at Moosejaw and the business of that subagency increased so very rapidly, because Moosejaw is at the western fringe of settlement, that it became necessary to establish an agency there. A large proportion of the business of the Regina agency was transacted through the Moosejaw office. Mr. Plaxton was subagent at Moosejaw, and, as in the case of other subagents, we were not presumed to be paying him a salary for the whole of his time. He had other occupations and only worked for us as a convenience and advantage to the settlement in that direction. When we established a land agency, we appointed an agent and did not appoint Mr. Plaxton. There was no connection between the two positions.
Am I to understand that Mr. Plaxton was not suspended?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
And that his services were entirely satisfactory ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am under the impression there was no complaint. The trouble was that the volume of business became so great that it did not appear right and proper that it should be handled through a subagency.

It seems to me that the proper man to appoint would be the man who had been carrying on the work of the subagency in a satisfactory manner and who had got in touch with the people. Another complaint was that the office was removed from a very convenient situation to one much less convenient to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is an error because there is very little difference between the location of the two. One was down a flight of stairs and the other is up a flight of stairs, and both are within a few doors of each other on the same street.
How many subagencies were closed in Manitoba during the past year ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say at the moment.
Why was the subagency at Ranchville closed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. W. J. Roche) asked the question in the House in the ordinary way, and, if I remember well, the answer was very much the same as I have given in the case of the question put by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Herron) except that in that case the subagent had not resigned. We felt that the settlement of that part of the country had progressed to such an extent that it was not necessary to keep up the subagency. There is no doubt that the subagency is a very great convenience. But we have to draw the line somewhere ; the House would not justify us in establishing subagencies everywhere or in keeping them open everywhere they have been established. The subland agency is more particularly a convenience in the newly-settled sections. A great deal of the business to be transacted with the land office by old settlers can be transacted by letter, whereas entry must be made in person and the presence of the subagency enables the entry to be made by the settler in the vicinity of the land. So, there is a reason for the subagency in the new territory that does not exist in the case of an old-settled section.

If the business had fallen off in this sub-agency, there would be force in what the minister has said. But I am informed that more business was done there last year than was done the year before. I know that the subagent has said-I have had no direct com-

munieation with him-that, judging by the business of 1907, there was more reason for maintaining the subagency than ever before. It was hardly necessary on the ground of economy to close the subagency, as the saving would be only $25 a month, I have had complaints from a number of the residents of the district concerning the closing of this office. A statement has been furnished me of the business of the office in February last. There were six entries for homesteads-proceeds $60-and implements, $15 ; three inspections were made ; there was one abandoned homestead, and there were thirty-two applications for patents. I think that this volume of business would compare favourably with that of any other subagency in Manitoba. Information with reference to the closing of this office has reached me as follows: The subagent, who in years gone by, was a very active politician, during the last provincial contest remained inactive. This did not please the Liberal candidate-who was defeated and who attributed his defeat not so much to the efforts of his political opponents as to the inactivity of the subagent. And it is no secret in that part of the country that this defeated candidate takes credit for having had this agent discharged because of his inactivity in the elections. If the information I have is correct, the business has not fallen off, but increased.
present land office; and I think I have shown that there was no good ground for closing this subagency.

Before the Moosejaw question passes, will the minister please tell us what special experience had Mr. Smith before his appointment as agent ? And also, I would ask him whether the minister does not consider that it would be more in the public interest, if, instead of closing subland offices and taking away the business for a week or more, it would have been better to make the transfer on the spot ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As to the office being closed down for a week or more, I can only say that it was an error. I do not know how it can be explained, but certainly it should not have been closed down for a week, whatever the explanation. As to the first question, I may explain that the agent's name is not Smith but Rutherford. I am not aware what experience he may have had with reference to land matters before he was made agent, but our experience of the conduct of that office since Mr. Rutherford's appointment has been eminently satisfactory. We believe we did not make any mistake in selecting either Mr. Rutherford or his staff. It may be to the credit of the staff, or it may be to the credit of the agent, but the office has been exceptionally well handled.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the committee will agree that the volume of business stated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. J. Roche) is hardly sufficient to justify the maintenance of this office. And, if this was an increase over that of previous months, I think it is pretty good evidence that instead of being wrong in closing the office when we did, if we had closed it sooner it would have been better in the interests of economy. But I admit that, once an office is established, it is difficult to get it closed. There is a certain amount of convenience to the public in having the office there, and there are always people who are offended and complain if it is closed. I do not wonder that there are complaints about the closing of this office any more than about the closing of the office at Pincher Creek. I have no hope of ever closing a subagency offic e without complaints being made, and yet I feel that we must close these offices from time to time ns settlement progresses.

The nearest agency is in the town of Dauphin, and the land agency in my own town of Minnedosa has been closed. The people in the section to which I have referred must go aeross the Riding mountains to Dauphin, or must go round by way of Neepawa a couple of hundred miles, or else by way of Roblin on the Canadian Northern. These people south of the Riding mountains are very inconveniently situated to reach the Mr. W. J. ROCHE.
When will the minister arrive at a policy with regard to forest reserve parks ? I have had some requests from men who wish to build hotels-temperance hotels, I may say-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What ?

I say, requests from parties wishing to build hotels at Waterton lake. I understand from the people of the department that the government has not arrived at a policy on that subject. When will the minister be able to state when and how these men can get permits or privileges to build ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As has been stated, we have hardly arrived at a definite policy in regard to these various reserves, because the conditions differ in each reserve. The particular matter to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) refers came before me some time ago, and if any gentleman desires to establish a resort within the limits of that park, I do not think there will be any serious difficulty in our coming to an arrangement if they make a proposition-we can come to an arrangement for a lease of the ground for a term of years. The Water-ton reserve, while, in terms, a forest reserve, is rather of the nature of a park, as it is reserved for park purposes rather than as a forest preserve. It completely surrounds with the Waterton lakes in the

Rocky mountains and is eminently suited for a park.

McCarthy. What new reserves have been made on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains within the last year ? I saw it stated in the newspapers in the west supporting the government that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) had said, at a meeting of the Forestry Association in Montreal, that all the east slope of the Rocky mountains from the national boundary to the northern limits of the country had been set aside as a forest reserve. Has the government made up its mind as to that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There must be "some error Somewhere, there has been no such reservation. There is of course the Waterton reservation.
What is the size of that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One or two townships. It is an old reservation set apart many years ago, and was never withdrawn from the departmental reservation. Then there is the Banff Park reservation, and there is also a large reservation at the Jasper House on the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That is about fifty miles in length from the southeast to the northwest, and extends from the foothills to the summit of the mountains. It will not be as large as the Banff park in area, because the Banff park, in its northeasterly portion, extends out far beyond the foothills of the Rockies. The railway will intersect it at about the centre. These are the only reservations that have been made on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. But at some future time further reservations may be made.
How many forest rangers are employed along the foothills from the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway near Banff to the boundary line-and I would like their names.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. W. I. Margacli, with headquarters at Calgary, has charge of the timber business between Calgary and the boundary line. He has the necessary authority to appoint fire rangers at $4 a day whenever, in his judgment, there is danger from fire. He authorizes them to take such measures as may be possible to guard'against fire. I have not a list of those fire guardians who are employed in that part of the country. They are merely temporary.

What check, if any, has the government upon these forest rangers as to the work they do, and the number of days they are employed? I understand that those employed on the Riding Mountains timber reserve are paid $4 a day. Is there any particular time of the year in which they are supposed to do this work ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The timber inspector who authorizes their employment, that is to say, who calls them out for service, checks their diary and certifies to their accounts. They keep a diary for the time they are out. Whenever the timber inspector thinks it is desirable that, in certain parts of the country, there should be one or more fire guardians on duty, he warns them out. They are local men. Of course he has a note of the day when they are supposed to start out. They keep a diary of their operations until they return. He examines these, and certifies to their accounts.
Do they send in any reports ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We get our reports from the inspector who sends these men out. We do not get individual reports from the fire rangers in the head office. They come to the local land office and are dealt with there.

The minister speaks about their being local men. I could understand why it is necessary to have local men. But I am aware of at least one man who cannot be considered a local man. He lives in a town at least fifteen or twenty miles from the nearest part of the Riding mountains. I looked up his account, and I find that last year he put in an account for 112 days. I do not know when he could get in those 112 days, because for months at a time he is never outside of the town, and the impression is that there is very little work secured by the government for the $4 a day.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is his name?
His name is Armitage. You will find it on L- 77.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is in the nature of things that there may be abuses in the method by which we carry on this business, but I do not know how we can check it down any better than we are doing. It will be admitted that it is not desirable that men should be on pay all the year round for a work of this kind. In some years there is a great deal of necessity for their services, and in other years there is no necessity at all. I think the only thing we can do is to keep a watch for abuses, and to remedy them whenever we find any to exist.

What is the German system?
Mr. OLIVER, The German system would not be applicable to the conditions under which we employ these men of whom I am speaking. That is to say that the men simply go out into the Crown lands and do what they can to prevent the starting or suppress the spread of fire.
Do you have a statutory declaration made by the ranger ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think so.
Do you not think it would be an additional check if he were to make a statutory declaration as to the distance he travelled and what he did ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is a very reasonable proposition, I will take it into consideration.
How many acres of school lands were sold in Manitoba last summer and how much money was realized from the sale ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the information at hand but I will obtain it.
Is there any definite time mentioned during which these sales shall be advertised and how they shall be advertised ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no time laid down in the law, as far as I am aware, but there is a custom which is followed with regard to the time and place of advertising and I do not think that custom has been deviated from.
Who was the auctioneer last summer in Manitoba ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My memory is that most of the sales were conducted by Mr. Norris.
Is the minister not aware that Mr. Ingram sold probably as much as Mr. Norris ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where the sales were not on a large scale I believe Mr. Ingram did make them. In order to ensure, in so far as we can ensure it, the sale to the highest bidder and a fair opportunity to every one to bid, the auctioneer should be under the control of the department. Mr. Ingram is a salaried official of the department who is particularly concerned in the school lands and we have thought that where the sale is not on such a large scale as to require additional assistance Mr. Ingram can very well act as auctioneer. We think that his position is such that we can feel assured that the work will be done fairly. But where the sale is on a larger scale, where Mr. Ingram will be needed to keep track of the books and where we have to employ an auctioneer we think it is better to employ only one auctioneer, a gentleman whom we think we can depend on and who may look forward to further employment if his work is satisfactory. I think we have employed Mr. Norris in a very large majority of cases.

Are these lands put up at the request of any particular persons or Mr. OLIVER.
under what circumstances are they advertised ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of course, the province is always glad to have the lands sold provided they are likely to bring a fair price. The decision as to their being offered for sale is arrived at by the Department of the Interior, opportunity being taken of the construction of railways and the settlement of the country concerned when we think that the land has reached, if not its maximum value, at any rate a fair value.
How is the auctioneer paid ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is paid by commission except that the amount must not be more than $200 on any one sale.
Did the government sell any land at Fort Saskatchewan last November ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I am informed there was no sale. There was a sale advertised, but the upset price was higher than the people seemed inclined to pay so that the sale was abortive.

The reason I asked that question is that I remember reading a report in one of the western papers to the effect that there was a sale advertised to take place at Fort Saskatchewan and the objection was urged that it was a very inopportune time for such a sale to take place, in the midst of the financial stringency when people generally would not be in a position to bid and also there was a misconception as to where the lands were situated. They were believed to be in the town site of Fort Saskatchewan, when, as a matter of fact, the lands were, I am informed, two miles out. The sale would have had the effect of reducing the price of lands and there was very strong objection' to the sale taking place at that time, the general belief being that the bidding would be eonfined to a few favoured individuals.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The sale did not take place. In answer to the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) I may say that the area of school land sold in Manitoba year was 102,761.70 acres and the price realized was $1,063,157.

I find the statement to which I referred the hon. Minister of the Interior some time ago about the announcement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture at the meeting of the Dominion Forestry Association, held in Montreal on March 12. The ' Calgary Morning Albertan' says :
Montreal, March 12.-The important announcement was made by the Hon. Sydney

Fisher at the Dominion Forestry Convention here to-day that the Dominion government had decided to set aside the whole eastern slope of the Rocky mountains forest area as forest reserve extending clear from the boundary to the extreme northern limit of the country. This vast region, he stated, would he kept free from settlers and held for forest growth which would be cut from time to time under such striot regulations as would preserve it for all time as a forest reserve for the west. The announcement was received with hearty cheers by the delegates.
That statement received a great deal of prominence throughout the press of Canada and I can hardly understand how it is that the Minister of Agriculture would be so reported if he did not make it. The impression has gone broadcast through the west that this was going to be done. Has the matter been discussed or is the minister at liberty to tell the committee if it has been under consideration ? I understand that some ten years ago there was a reservation along the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains and that It was subsequently thrown open, I am given to understand, on the advice or suggestion of the Minister of the Interior. Apparently the Minister of Agriculture must have had some authority for making that statement because we could hardly suspect that he would force himself upon the Department of the Interior and make any such statement as that when there was no foundation for it.
Mr. OLIVER, I think there must be some misunderstanding. For instance in one point the Minister of Agriculture is quoted as saying that it was the intention of the government to make a reservation along the whole eastern slope of the Rocky mountains from the boundary line to either the northern part of Alberta or of the Dominion. My hon. friend is aware that the slope of the Rocky mountains after a certain point is not under the jurisdiction of this government but of the government of British Columbia. As to the fact of their being a general reservation, such as my hon. friend has mentioned, I understand there was some suggestion of such a reservation but I did not understand that it was ever made.

It is another Instance of the Minister of Agriculture butting into some one else's department. He has not fared as well in this case as in the Militia Department, because the Minister of the Interior does not propose to back up his statement in regard to this reservation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a matter between the Minister of Agriculture and the newspapers, not between the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of the Interior.

It shows conclusively that the Minister of the Interior proposes to run his own department.
319i

The matter is important in two ways. I remember distinctly the announcement having been made at a great meeting in Montreal by the Minister of Agriculture, and I remember that all the newspapers heartily approved of the idea of what they thought to be, from the minister's statement, an accomplished fact, namely the reservation of the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. It is strange indeed that the Minister of Agriculture should go to Montreal and before a very representative gathering from every part of the Dominion make that authoritative statement on behalf of the Dominion government and then, three or four months afterwards, when we come to question the Minister of the Interior who has it in charge he says that no such thing has been done and if I understand him rightly that no such thing has been discussed with any practical idea of carrying it out at the present time. That is a very reprehen-sive proceeding on the part of one minister of the government and, as my friend has just said, it is not the first time that the Minister of Agriculture seems, to have spoken very recklessly and entirely apart from the record. If it was not done, it certainly was in harmony with all the resolutions passed during the last ten years by the forestry meetings, and by what we may call in Canada the authorities on forestry. I remember that in this House not long ago a speech was made by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of the Interior in which he took up as one branch of this subject the question of forest reserves and showed the immense importance of having forest reserves made and made quickly so that there should not be any longer delay. He was good enough to refer at that time to some remarks made in the House some months before on the same subject, and I understood that the government and the Minister of the Interior very heartily subscribed to those ideas as they were brought out in the general discussion in the House. If the minister has done nothing it rather goes to support what was said in the debate in the House some four months ago that whilst information has been ' being gathered ' and while the statements have been favourable to such a policy the Dominion government is letting year after year pass practically without doing anything. Of course it is of no use to have forest reserves unless the government at the same time go in for a system of preserving the water flow of the country as well, that is setting apart the reservoir sites so that the waters which would otherwise be wasted in overflows might be preserved and be made very useful in the later time when the water was more necessary. The minister knows very well that the United States government has spent millions of money and inaugurated a really wonderful policy in that direction

taking hold of the forest slopes and of the arid regions and by a system of water dams or reservoirs really turning millions of acres, formerly arid and of no use, into very eligible lands which they are selling at a large advance and out of which they will recoup themselves for all the expenses they have gone to and more. But what is of more importance is that at the same time they are keeping the forest reserves and turning arid lands into splendid agricultural lands and thus filling up the country with a very eligible population who go to these lands and do small farming in a tidy and intensive way, making themselves the best producing citizens in the agricultural line.	,
The minister to-day tells us that there are only three reserves, one of them the Banff, which we have had ever since we remember anything almost in our Northwest history, then this little picayune Waterton one, a township or a township and a half which really can hardly be called a reservation and the other one intersected by the National Transcontinental Railway. Those are the three at the present time and that is all we have. Does the minister not think that this is one of the most important questions that could engage the attention of his department and does he not think that most valuable time is passing while he is doing nothing ? Is there not the possibility that the timber areas and water supplies will have passed into the hands of private parties before the government inaugurates a comprehensive policy of reserves ? The minister comes from the west and knows that there is nothing which so agitates the people of that country and will agitate them as this very question. I read a most striking statement by Professor Robertson not more than three weeks ago in which he really called a halt to this self-glorification in which we have been indulging as to the mighty things we are doing in the west. He pointed out that we are in reality doing nothing in the west except shearing the fleece off and making no return or preparation for subsequent growth, that there is nothing like intensive farming and really no proper guarding of the reserves in water, forests and coal ; but that we are simply taking all that comes in sight and laying up no reserve force for a rainy day. That process has taken place in the United States and the United States government has only recently, under President Roosevelt, taken up that large and broad system of 'reserves and of bringing in to the assistance of nature, nature's forces, which heretofore have been allowed to go to waste or to become destructive.
Now, we in Canada cannot commence too soon in that business. The fertility of our Northwest depends on our taking care of our forest reserves and looking after our Mr. POSTER.
resources of moisture. In the southern states and throughout the western states the immense losses from sudden overflows are year after year becoming more and more onerous, and men who give their attention to the subject point out that these losses arise very largely from the denudation of the forest areas. We cannot commence at this work too early; yet I am afraid that the minister is pottering around on non-essentials instead of giving full force to this very important consideration. Some one persuades him to build out here a sort of castle of Chillon in which to immure fifteen or sixteen astronomers who will try to discover a new ring around a planet or the tail of a comet in some far-off nebula. $150,000 has gone into that venture; but $150,000 put into this other matter would yield greater results to this country, and the stars might be allowed to cavort around a little longer without being subjected to the inspection of peering eyes. A man comes to a minister with a telegram, and we build a mint, and spend $600,000 on it; and now we have the mint, and we shall have the loss for ever and a day. In the meantime our western country is crying out for the preservation of those things which are essential to its growth and its continued prosperity. The minister is not doing much, though he is doing something. He takes particular trouble to secure a herd of three or four hundred buffalo at immense expense. It is nice to have the buffalo, but they will not form water reservoirs or keep the forest tracts of the country where they should be. All these things have their proper place, but it seems to me that if we neglect this matter of forest preservation, we neglect the greater thing while bestowing a great deal of pains and cost upon subsidiary things.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: A mistake has possibly arisen from confusing the two words reservation and preservation. There is not much difference in the words themselves, but there is a vast difference in the meaning of the words.
One is necessary to the other, isn't it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is where my hon. friend and I do not altogether see, alike. My hon. friend seems to think that reservation is preservation. I do not think that it is necessarily so. With regard to the preservation of the forest areas along the eastern slope of the Rocky -mountains, I would not wish my hon. friend to suppose that the subject has not been considered ; but it has been considered with this in view, that we have a Forest Reserve Act passed with a view to certain conditions, and we find that the conditions prevailing along the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains are such as hardly to make it advisable to apply the provisions of that Act along the

whole slope. We have there deposits of coal ot stupendous amount and value- but they are of no value unless they are operated, and the purpose of the government is, so far as it has any connection with the matter, to secure their operation to the limit. We want as much of them as possible operated as soon as possible. I think I am safe in saying that that is the view taken by the government.
As much as is necessary for the country's need.
