speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As much as is possible to be operated; because we believe that we have coal to spare to all the world, and that the operation of these coal measures for an outside market would add greatly to the wealth and prosperity of our country /and not do ourselves any harm. If the little country of England, with its stupendous population and its stupendous industrial requirements, all dependent on the use of coal, as ours are not, owing to our water-powers, can afford to ship coal to all the world that will buy it-and it is as a matter of fact shipped to all the world, even to its most remote corners-we in Canada with a coal supply in comparison with which that of the British Isles is insignificant, can very well afford to take the same view and make what money we can out of our coal as opportunity offers. That is at any rate my personal view at the present time. The application of our Forest Reserves Act and its limitations to the area to which we look for the operation of our coal measures would be a clash of interests. It would interfere with the operation of our coal measures and the general industrial development along the base of the Rocky mountains. That, however, does not exclude a policy of forest preservation or of reforestation with a view to preserving both the water supply and the supply of timber. With this explanation my hon. friend will see that there is not so very much difference between the statement as It appears in the newspaper and the statement I presented to the House. As I said a few moments ago, the hon. gentleman seems to think that reservation is preservation. On that point I want to take very direct issue with him. We must give opportunity for the investment of capital and the application of energy, enterprise and intelligence in the turning to account of our natural resources, or our natural resources are worth nothing to anybody. They are not worth reserving or preserving unless there is capital and intelligence and energy and opportunity to a reasonable degree to turn them to account. In the United States at the present time and under present conditions, with the stupendous development of population, of wealth, of industry which has taken place in that country, after having shorn the fleece of 99-100 of its value, they
may very well turn round and adopt a policy of preservation, or reservation if you like, in regard to the balance. The time has come when that may very well be a leading policy of the government of that country. Had that policy been adopted when the United States had only a population of 5,000,000 people, had it been then announced that there would be a policy of reservation for the sake of preserving the natural resources of that country throughout all its vast area, we would have had to wait several thousand years for the development that has taken place. There has been a waste, if you like to call it so, of the natural resources of the United States, but there has been there the most phenomenal development the world has ever seen; and I am under the impression that, for the present at any rate, while we should have due care for the preservation of our natural resources, we should also see that there is ample opportunity for the employment of capital and labour in the development of those resources and in turning them to account as contributions to the wealth and prosperity of the country.

At the risk of taking up a few moments more I want to put another view. I do not agree with my hon. friend in the main. I still hold that reservation is absolutely necessary for preservation. I do not mean that the government should stretch its hand over every bit of natural resources we have and lock them up from any private or corporate development. That would be the climax of absurdity. But if you are going to preserve a sufficient amount of our natural resources, you have to begin now. Suppose you give to every corporation and individual with capital to invest all our natural resources, suppose you hurry to put every bit into their hands, what will you have for the state? Now is the time for the government to decide what it ought to reserve and reserve that portion. My hon. friend says, speaking of coal, that the government cannot make these reservations because there are coal areas upon them. But it is quite possible to reserve your coal areas and administer them as they ought to be administered. I do not think it should be the policy of any government to get as many of those coal areas as possible into the hands of capitalists. these are the country's own resources and the country has a perfect right to their usufruct. As they belong to the people, the people have the right to parcel them out as they please with the object of letting the people have at least its fair share of the profits. It is not necessary to give capital all the profit from these areas in order to have them developed. Mr. Whitney did not take that view, and his policy has been of great advantage to the province of Ontario. Under the old policy, the mining areas were sold

-at $3 an acre. Whoever applied for them *and complied with the conditions got them *at that rate. Mr. Whitney reserved, however, certain portions of the Cobalt area absolutely to the government and allowed no prospecting upon them. He had them prospected himself, through the government officers, and there is not the least doubt that there is a patrimony stored up in those reservations of millions and millions of dollars which will ultimately go into the treasury of Ontario. Is not that the proper policy? But if my hon. friend s contentions were carried out, Mr. t\ hitney would sell these areas at $3 an acre in order to bring in capital for the development. Take Cobalt Lake, for instance; there was supposed to be beneath the lake, which is 25 to 40 feet in depth, mineral leads of different qualities, because all along the sides these leads had been prospected. If the old government had been in office, under its policy the 40 acres would have been sold for $120. But Mr. Whitney did not do that. He put them up for sale and tender and he got $1,087,000. And there was no difficulty in getting capital to come in. My hon. friend asked what would the United States have been if they had adopted such a policy? Why, the wealth of the United States people would be to-day immeasurably greater than it is if thirty or fifty years ago they had reserved a propel portion of their natural resources in timber lands, coal lands and mineral lands and had kept them until the present to be operated by corporations or private parties or the state as they might think best. A-nd the one thing which the best people in the United States deplore to-day in connection with this great question of capital and labour-the few rich and the many poor-is the improvidence of the state m having put too much its great natural resources into private hands instead of keeping them for the public good and giving the people their share of the profits. My hon. friend is anxious to get the coal areas in the Northwest opened up so that we may export our coal into every country in the world. I do not think that any well-wisher to the people is anxious for such consummation. He says that Great Britain has been exporting its coal a century and more. So it has, but to-day the British people are up against a coming failure of their fuel supply, and before many years you will find the people of England very chary of selling for export the only available fuel reserves they have. Canada is supposd to exist for more than a hundred years, for more than twenty-five centuries, and I am not at all anxious that we should too rapidly use up our coal reservations in the Northwest by sending out our coal to every country in the world in order to realize immediate profit. Our great natural resources are as much a national defence as the arms which we put into the hands of our soldiers. In this Mr. FOSTER.
great competition between nation and nation, when coal is the only fuel we have left, the last thing in the world that Canada should do is to denude itself of its coal areas. If we should, future generations will curse the policy which disembowelled the earth of its fuel resources and distributed them to strangers for the sake of the little profit obtained at the time.
I believe that a country has just as good a right to defend itself by keeping its great coal area to itself, and its pulpwood and timber to itself-for the same remark applies to these-as it has to engage in any other defensive measure. Why should we hurry and rush to get our timber cut down and exported in exchange for a small sum of money, when, for centuries to come, our own people in increasing numbers will want timber ? Rather we should regard this as a fund held in trust for the whole of Canada for the whole of the future, and we should make it a policy that not one stick of timber shall be taken off without making sure that another is growing to replace it. Reforestation rather than a spendthrift destruction for export of these natural resources should be the policy of the country. I invite my hon. friend to think over these things in the night watches, to consider what I have said and see if he cannot revise his opinion, and, by all means, get a hustle on and reserve these water resources, timber resources and mineral resources as far as proper. One thing more I ivould like to ask him : Is he taking any steps in regard to the large forest areas that have already gone into private hands, so as to have regulations made by which these forests shall be perpetually kept up ? They have been granted, and for a song, and it will add, of course, to the value of the grant if the government makes regulations which make the supply perpetual; but the country has so great an interest in the matter that I 'would rather see this than see it left in the hands of these speculators to denude these areas of their timber. I think the minister ought, with all the wisdom there is in his department, to give his attention to how it is possible to preserve every acre of timber and prevent it being denuded, keeping it as a perpetual producer for the benefit of the people of this country, even though the benefit inures directly to the individuals who, at the present time, are the fortunate possessors.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has placed a proposition before the House, as it appeals to my mind, of having you cake and eating it. I do not think he has been able to make clear how that end is to be arrived at. He said that, if the United States fifty years ago, had adopted a policy of reservation in regard to its natural resources, that country

would have beea vastly richer to-day. We cannot tell what would have been the case had a certain policy been adopted fifty years ago. But I submit that the most valuable asset of the United States-admitted in all the rest of the world and admitted in the United States as well-is the individuality, the energy, the enterprise, the industry of the people of the United States. And, had it been the policy of the government of the United States at any stage of the history of that country-a policy which, of course, would have been impossible in the temper of the people-to put up the bars against the exercise of the energy, enterprise and inventive spirit of the people there could not have been the development, the prosperity, the success that there has been. It is because the forests have been cut down, it is because the earth has been 1 disembowelled of its coal ' and of its iron, it is because these natural resources have been turned to the uses of man that the United States is as it is today. Take the case of Ontario, this very country. Given conditions as they are on the continent of America to-day outside of the province of Ontario, and the province of Ontario would be more valuable if it were covered with the trees with which it was covered a hundred years ago than denuded of its trees as it is to-day. But had the province of Ontario and the rest of the continent remained (covered with trees during all these years, there would have been no value in the province of Ontario to-day. You must give opportunity to the application of energy, intelligence, enterprise and industry, or you have no value. What I am trying to impress upon the minds of hon. members is that the natural resource has not, of itself, any value, it is made of value by the application of the energy, intelligence and industry of man in supplying the needs of man-in that way and in no other. There is a time coming-it has no doubt come in the history of the United States, and it is coming in the history of Canada-when there will be a sufficient aggregation Of accumulated wealth and of population and of surplus energy, for a policy of reservation and preservation and special care of the natural resources that remain to be entered upon. But I submit that the fact that this time has arrived in the history of the United States is no evidence that it has arrived in the history of Canada. It is, however, a fact that we should be unworthy of our position if we did not learn by the experience of others. Recognizing what has taken place there, we may recognize also what has been done to couple preservation with enterprise, and that is the object of our policy at the present time. We hope to achieve a reasonable measure of preservation of our natural resources so that they may be turned to useful account, but it is not to the degree suggested at any rate by
my hon. friend a policy of reservation that would prevent them being turned to account by the energy, enterprise and industry of our people. To get away from generalities, and to deal now with matters of more detail, speaking of our policy in regard to coal, under the regulations by which the coal lands of the west are administered at the present time, we do not contemplate the alfenation of these areas except on condition that they shall be operated.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Tnat is the present policy ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Within what time must they be operated ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Within a year from notice given by the government.

On lease.
(Mr. OLIVER. Yes, and the lease is conditioned upon their being operated within a year from notice given by the government. That is the point I want to -show-the difference between reservation and preservation, between reservation and development. We are not handing out-as I think my hon. friend suggested-the coal areas of the country to private hands; we are holding them in the hands of the government until the time arrives when they can be worked at a profit. And then our policy is that the opportunity shall be there to the firstcomer, the first man who is prepared to take them over upon the terms upon which we otter them which terms involve their operation.
Have you increased the size of the area that may be given to one individual under the new system of leasing instead of selling ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Our regulations do not provide for granting more than four sections to one individual, but they do provide that several individuals may combine their interests. When we sold, we onjy sold half-sections.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In the form of lease you adopt, is there a certain ground rental and a royalty ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. The ground rent is $1 an acre a year ; the royalty is five cents a ton.
Can that be raised by the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think not during the terms of the lease.
Is there any system of computation as to acreage payment and royalty payment ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A coal lease is available to the first comer who will accept it on the conditions. We place a ground rent upon the land so that there will be no inducement to any one to hold it unless he

operates it, and the condition of operation is a condition of tlie lease, upon notice being' given. In regard to timber, the condition is somewhat different from that imposed in regard to coal. It is possible that for one reason or another the supply of timber within a section of country may at some future period become exhausted. It is also to be remembered that the timber supply may be renewed while the coal supply cannot. Therefore it is proper that any policy dealing with the disposition of the timber should have as a part of that policy the reproduction of the forest. That is, I may say, a part of the policy of this government, although not yet developed as highly as we hope it will be at some later time. But there are many things to learn in regard to this matter. We have not yet been able to form a scientific system with regard to the widely varying conditions prevailing over our vast territory. We may be going too slowly, but we have to consider the public purse, and we do not like to ask for large sums until we feel that we can assure parliament that we are going to get value for the expenditure. The timber which is under the control of the Dominion government, I may say, is but a comparatively small part of the total timbered area of Canada. Under the previous regulations the principle was the same as that which prevails in regard to coal, that is to say, that the first comer got it on application, subject of course to sale by tender. But now we hold practically the whole of our timber under reservation, and we only offer it for sale when we are satisfied that the public interest requires it. That is an important difference between the former system and the present one. Formerly our timber was open to the first applicant. We did not have to put it up, it is true, but our practice was that tffe timber wTas offered to the first applicant. Now we advertise it to the world when we think that the public interest will best be served by putting up any part of it. This system actually places the timber under reservation.
In regard to the reproduction of the forests, or the reforesting of the present forest area, let me say that while the forest is valuable and while the reproduction of the forest is valuable, the land is also valuable for agriculture. Where there is an area of country that to-day is covered by mercantable timber that is required for the use of the people and when that timber is cleared off the land is valuable for farming purposes, it is a question whether we would be warranted in all cases in insisting upon the reforesting of the area cut off. It is no secret that the Dominion of Canada, in its stupendous area, is not all fertile. We have, it is true, vast areas that are fertile ; but I do not think I can be charged with decrying the country when I say that there are also vast areas that are not suitable for agri-Mr. OLIVER.
culture, but which, in many cases, are covered by timber and in some cases by timber of great value. Now under these circumstances if there are immense areas of country covered by timber the land of which is of agricultural value when the timber is cleared off. it would be a fair proposition to say that we should limit our efforts at reforestration to some extent at least, to those areas that are not valuable, or less valuable for agricultural purposes. That is the policy of the government. There is in the railway belt of British Columbia where the greater part of the timber supply is situated which is under the control of this government, very limited areas of most valuable agricultural land which is to-day covered by timber of great value. There is, however, in that same area a very large proportion of the land covered by timber, which land is of much less agricultural value. My view is that when the timber is cleared off land that is of especial agricultural value, we should not undertake to reforest it. At the same time we should have a well defined and aggressive policy of reforestation, and I will be glad to bring before the House such a policy as soon as we have information at hand, and are able to present to the government a system that we would be warranted in asking the House to support. I wish to confine our efforts at reforestation to the vast area in the railway belt which is of lesser value for agricultural purposes. The same policy will be applied to the three prairie provinces. Where the laud is not suited for agricultural purposes it may be very well adapted to reforestation, init where it is suited for agriculture it seems to me that the greater value is achieved by employing it for purely agricultural purposes because, after all, there is plenty of land callable of producing timber and good timber that is not of great value for agricultural purposes.

There is a distinction between the different, classes of natural resources which illustrates the difference between reservation and preservation. Timber is a natural resource that reproduces itself while mineral is a natural resource that does not reproduce itself. Therefore, where we have a natural resource which reproduces itself preservation will meet the full requirements of the case without any general system of reservation. If proper regulations are enacted governing the cutting of timber there is no question whatever, that, if you provide a proper fire guarding system, the present supply of timber in the country will be maintained throughout the years that are to come. But, it is important that there should not only be proper regulations with regard to the cutting of timber, but that these regulations should be stringently enforced. Having had some experience wi+h resrard to timber, I see no

objection whatever to the leasing of the timber limits of the country under proper conditions. The difficulty has been in the United States that the men who have been engaged in the lumber business have thought only of the present and have, in taking out the larger timber, destroyed the smaller growth which eventually would make the larger timber and the fact that in the United States there is not a very great timber supply has made it necessary for them to adopt a general reforestation system. I think that at the present time in this country it is not necessary_ and it will not be necessary if we adopt and carry out proper regulations for the preservation of timber. Therefore, I am to a considerable extent of the same view as that which the minister has expressed with regard to the timber supply of the country. I think, that the minister should apply himself to the working out of a proper system of regulations. The regulations we have, in fact, at the present time, are not so bad if they are properly carried out and I think that this question of the timber supply and of the water supply, consequent upon the forest being maintained, will not be a serious question for at least many years to come in this country.
In so far as the coal in the west is concerned, I do not think we need, for many years to come, have a great deal of fear about exhausting the supply. I would be glad to see every ton of coal that is produced in this country used for the production of manufactures so that we would not be shipping out one ton of coal and so that it would not be shipping out a natural product but a product in its manufactured state. But, under the conditions as they are at present, that is not possible and therefore I do not think it would be advisable for us to enact legislation which would prevent coal owners from shipping to foreign countries. We hope the time will come when we can employ all our coal at home because it is a great advantage to us if we can use all our iron, coal, and limestone in the manufacture of steel and iron, but at the present time, I think it would be a suicidal policy for us to say that no coal shall be exported. On the coast of British Columbia the tremendous amount of labour which is employed to-day in the mining of coal, because the coal owners are allowed to ship south when they have no coal, would be turned out of employment if legislation of that sort were enacted. I think that the present policy is an excellent one, that the coal areas should no longer be absolutely alienated but that they should be leased, the Crown retaining control. I think that policy is all right. Perhaps it is not well that there should be an absolute figure fixed for the royalty which cannot be increased. I think that the government should have the power to make a general increase in the royalty. Again, on that question of royalty
it does seem to me that the ease or difficulty with which the mine can be operated ought to have some effect upon the amount of royalty which a man should pay because it has a great effect upon the profit that would be produced from a mine and there should be a sliding scale. I can understand how difficulties might creep in and how favouritism might be used in this case but it seems to me that a distinction should be made, that a sliding scale should be adopted.
I would like to ask the minister if he has received many applications for the leasing of coal lands under the new regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: 1 cannot give the number. We have not had nearly as great a demand for leases as we have had for purchases, but still we have had a very considerable demand. I will give the figures later.

With regard to the regulations governing the leasing of coal lands, my opinion is that it would be utterly impossible to get coal lands in the Northwest leased under these regulations because of their stringency. Every' one knows that in coal mining, a large amount of capital is required and if you say to a man: You can have these coal lands, but you must agree to operate them, to pay a royalty and to give up your lease at the expiration of twenty-one year's, you lay down conditions that will make it utterly impossible to get these coal lands taken up and operated. Twenty-one years in the life of a coal mine is nothing at all.
The leases are renewable?
The regulations do not say so. It is entirely at the option of the Governor in Council.
It is the usual way.

It is the usual way, but we have to take what they say. A man will not make a large investment if he can only have a lease of coal lands for twenty-one years. The business is one which requires hundreds and thousands of dollars and in my opinion it will be utterly impossible to get the coal lands operated.
The timber leases are only from year to year; yet they are considered to be perpetual.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One of the objections that our hon. friends opposite take to the present leases is that there is a provision made that on the fulfilment of certain conditions which are set out the lease will continue so long, as there is timber on the limit.
I do not think there is any such provision with regard to coal mining leases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

I have consulted men who have been operating mines on Vancouver Island with reference to extending their business to the Northwest and they have refused to take any interest i(n these coal areas under the present regulations. As to the contention of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) with reference to the reservation of coal lands, if that were carried out we would not have any coal mined in British Columbia to-day. The principle laid down by the hon. gentleman was that we should simply hand over coal areas in proportion to the demand of the home market. The British Columbia coal mines have developed simply on account of the foreign market which they supplied. Seventy-five per cent of the production of coal in British Columbia to-day is depending on a foreign market. Not a dollar would have been invested in coal mining in British Columbia had it not been that the capitalists who went into these ventures knew that they had a market in the United States. The development of the Crow's Nest Pass mines proceeded upon the assumption that their principal market was in the United States. Of the coal of Vancouver Island for many years 98 per cent found a market in the United States. If the principle advocated by my hon. friend were carried out it would be impossible to operate mines. By operating mines you increase your home market. As a matter of fact within six or eight years in Vancover Island the home market for coal has increased from 10 per cent to 50 per cent; half of the coal of the island is going into the home market by reason of the development of British Columbia, especially the Pacific coast. According to the principle of my hon. friend the coal will have to remain there until you have a home market when, as a matter of fact, it is the operation of coal mines with the increased population and development of manufactures that creates the home market.
I would like the minister 'to consider the possibility of making extensive changes in the coal regulations. Under the existing regulations they have to operate, they have to pay a royalty and they have a lease for -twenty-one years which may or may not be renewed according to the good will of the Governor in Council, which I am informed will prevent the development and operation of coal mines.

I did not know that the leases were for 21 years only. The royalty,
I consider, is all right; perhaps an acreage royalty might be collected. I think you should have the leases renewable because as my hon. friend has pointed out the operation of coal mines calls for enormous capital. You cannot equip a mine to produce 700 or 800 tons a day without the expenditure of $300,000 or $400,000. If a man has to invest $300,000 and after 21 Mr. OLIVER
years he might be at the mercy of Tiberius, he will be in a serious condition and will not put his money in. You will remove the worst objection if you make the lease renewable.
If all conditions are fulfilled.

If all conditions are fulfilled of course, and if the conditions are not fulfilled, you should have the right to enter at any time and take possession of the property. As to the area I do not believe that four sections are enough.
Hear, hear.
The person going into the business has to get the names of fictitious persons to apply for leases. _
They may be genuine names but the leases may be assigned.

But they may not have any interest in the matter. We know that is the case. It is done all around. When we used to sell coal lands, the area wras only 320 acres and of course you had to get people to assign them. I think it better to make the limit double that amount, eight sections. When you are going to invest $300,000 or $400,000, four sections is a small area to work. Coal mining is not all profit, I have had some experience and know that it requires a very large amount of money.
I understand that according to these regulations the price at which coal is to be supplied to settlers in the district is fixed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: To settlers in the vicinity.
Did the coal leases granted by the Crown contain such a provision ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, yes. It was because the previous regulation contained that provision that it was continued in the present regulation, not because I had any personal belief in its merits.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That period of 21 years does seem a very short term on which to invite the investment of ajarge amount of money in the development and operation of coal mines. The system under the Nova Scotia lease is for a term of 20 years with provision for three renewals, so that the total term reaches SO years, after which the government is not obliged to renew, although, I suppose, under ordinary conditions they would certainly do so. There are also two important provisions in the Nova Scotia statute, section 46, chapter 18 of the revised statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900:
Every lease shall contain a provision that the royalties may be increased, diminished or otherwise changed by the legislature.
And in respect to the renewals to which I referred, it contains this provision :

In any such renewal the rent payable by such lessee may be increased under the authority of this chapter or of any such statute, subject to the provsions of the next following section.
Under this provision the royalty might be increased at the end of each 20 year period. It seems to me that some such system as that would be a good one to adopt in regard to coal lands in the west.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the present regulations were adopted I had in view the operation of coal lands in the prairie rather than in the mountains. The operation of coal mines where the seams are horizontal and regular and the distance below the surface is not great does not require such a large investment. I will confess that I had not in mind, to the degree that I should have had, the application of these regulations to the mountains where the seams are irregular and where the expense of installation of a mining plant is stupendously greater. However, as these are regulations and not statutes it is a matter that can be very easily adjusted, and I may say that the very great demand that was being made for coal lands under the recent regulations seemed to me to have outrun the probability of development to such an extent that I did not think the interest of the country were going to suffer seriously under the new regulations until we had at any rate plenty of time to see them experimentally in operation and to see where the faults and failings lie. I do not presume to be able to foresee every condition and I am very grateful for the suggestions that have been made to me. They have struck me also in this way. The Canadian Pacific Railway have a very valuable coal mine in operation in the Banff park under conditions as to lease and they have a lease for a term of 20 or 21 years. .Everybody knows that they have made a large expenditure and are operating a very useful mine. They are intending to eniarge their operations and require the investment of a still larger capital, but in looking for further capital to increase their operations they bump into the restriction of a 21 year lease. They say to us : We would like to get the privilege of a renewal of this lease and unless we can get that privilege we cannot secure the larger investment that we desire to make, and that is desirable in order that the country should get the full benefit of the coal measures there. Thus the matter has been brought very pointedly to my attention and I think in time we will be able to remedy the difficulty.
Is there any distinction between the anthracite and the ordinary bituminous coal under the regulations ?

We have not under our present regulations. The former regulations made a difference, the anthracite was sold at $20 an acre while the ordinary coal was sold at $10 an acre. I do not think it would be advisable to provide for changes in the royalty, at any rate during the term of the lease. I think it would be very proper to arrange that there should be a renewal of the lease, and that at that time the royalty might be changed, but I do not think it would be a proper inducement to capital to hold out the possibility of the royalty being changed during the term of the lease. It would be very much better, if you ask people to invest their money in the enterprise, that you should let them know exactly what the ground rent and the royalty are, during a reasonable period, at any rate. If I were willing to concede any change, it would be in regard to the ground rent rather than the royalty. I may assume that the regulations, as far as they have come under criticism as yet, are reasonably satisfactory and I shall certainly take account of the representations that have been made in regard to the extension of the term.
Will the royalty be applied to all companies which are now operating mines?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
The government propose, however, to levy a royalty on all Hew mines?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I think the principle is a good one from the beginning, but it rather places the late developer at a disadvantage, because he will be called on to pay a royalty while some of those operating large mines obtained some time ago will not be, and so their coal will cost so much less. I have been written to in regard to this matter of discriminating against the men who now invest their capital, but I presume that the policy has been adopted by the department as being in the best interests of the country and of coal development. With regard to the leasing regulations that have been adopted, I have heard very much the same sentiment as that expressed by the bon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), that the term of twenty-one years is somewhat short. I can understand the desire of the minister to check some of the applications that were made at large in years gone by in regard to coal lands. At the same time, I would point out that under the leasing system lie is practically placing all the coal lands in the hands of men with capital and beyond the reach of the prospector. Under the old system, which I admit had its abuses, the man who went into the hills and searched out these minerals and who could get to-

gether some of his friends and form a syndicate to purchase a tract of land for coal mining purposes, had some advantage. I do not like the idea of cutting out the prospector. With regard to the twenty-one year lease, I understand that the lease price is a dollar an acre. That means that for the term you are paying $21 an acre for your coal lands, or, if the lease is renewed for another term, $42, and by the time it is renewed for 99 years you are paying a pretty high figure for your coal. If it is decided to be the best policy to continue the leasing principle, I quite concur in the propriety of including in the lease a provision by which the lessee would know that at the end of the period, if he had conformed with the regulations, his lease would be renewed for a further period. I would also favour some reduction in the charge per acre.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The point which my hon. friend has mentioned in regard to the prospector is certainly a very important point, and it is one on which I feel quite as keenly as he does, and I am not sure that we might not be able to make some change in the regulations to avoid cutting out the prospector. But at the time the regulations were passed, I think everybody will agree, the prospector was rather overdoing a very good thing-he was getting in his deadly work at a rate which the country could not stand, and it was necessary to cut him off short. However, I appreciate the prospector and the value of his work, and I can assure the House that he shall get every possible consideration at my hands.
I think after all that the prospector will not be very much the worse. Previously he had to buy the land, now he can lease his four sections.
He cannot dispose of it in the same way.

But still we must look at what is going to be in the general interest of the country. Perhaps the government will employ prospectors. I think they ought to do that, to find out where these coal lands are, because they are going to get a larger income from them.
Mr. FOSTER, I see the Minister of Agriculture has come in, and I think I will renew the matter that we could not decide during his absence. For his information I may say that in the course of the information that has been given us, it was stated by the Minister of the Interior that no reservation had been made or was contemplated of the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains. The hon. member for Calgary informed the Minister of the Interior that the Minister of Agriculture had some months ago in the city of Montreal announced to the Forestry Association that the government had reserved or was on the eve of reserving the whole of the east-
ern slope of the Rocky mountains, and great applause was given to the minister and to the government for undertaking that policy.

I have the honour of representing a district where I think the largest coal areas are to be found and the greatest quantity of coal mines of any portion of the Dominion. I shall not take up time by repeating what has been well said by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) and Kings (Mr. Fowler) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden). But I wish to emphasize the fact that the development of new mining has practically been brought to a standstill by the system of leasing. The minister may have had many applications for leases of new coal lands but they are nearly all in connection with some coal lands already in operation. Were it not for that, I think I am safe in saying that he would not have had any applications whatever for the leasing of coal areas. I wish to point out the disadvantage a man is under who has only a lease. It is impossible for him to get capital to any extent to open up his coal mine, under the lease system, when the government practically only grant a lease for twenty-one years. The prospector has therefore quit looking over coal. Dozens of men know where there are large coal fields, who do not think it worth while to apply for them under the present system. It is quite true that there were great abuses under the old system but the new system has gone to the opposite extreme. Where a man complies with the conditions of the lease, it would be very easy to continue it. It would be very easy to give him a guarantee that if he complies with the conditions made from time to time by the government, he would be assured of a continuance of the lease for a longer period. It takes a very large amount of capital to develop a coal mine. One company in my riding whose mine has been in operation only four years, has put in two sets of machinery, their last set cost them over $400,-
000.	Another company has spent in developing work mostly, in the way of machinery and a railway, over $4,000,000. It is impossible to develop a mine without from $250,000 up to several millions, and no one will risk that money under the present lease system. I would recommend the minister to make some provision by which, if a man is going to open up a mine, he will have a lease for a longer period than twenty-one years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it will be found that the lease system is not so much against operation as against speculations. One of the most highly developed coal properties in the west has been developed under the lease system in the Banff park. This is the Anthracite coal property, now oper-

ate<l by the Canadian Pacific Railway. True they would be better off if they had a longer lease or if I could arrange so that they would have a longer lease ; but the fact nevertheless remains that out of the five or six mountain mines now in operation, this one is under lease and has the most thoroughly equipped plant of them all.
That was long before the present regulation,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes,' under regulations which applied to Banff- park alone. Those regulations are to a great extent the basis of the regulations now applicable to the whole country.
Is the lease the same as at present 1

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Practically the same.
Mi'. GALLIHER. As to time ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, it does not provide for a renewal, but I think the difficulty can be overcome in the case by legislation. If I should come down with a Bill asking for an amendment, my hon. friends will understand that the question has been already before the House. There have been leases issued to the number of sixty-four since the 15th June, 1907, under the present regulations. Quite true, a good many were in order to add to property already held under purchase; but, on the other hand, there are also a number of applications for leases, for operation as separate mines. True it is that the inducements which formerly existed to prospect for coal-that is to say the speculative inducement-does not exist to-day; and I am free to admit that that speculative inducement was a right and proper, and up to a certain time, necessary feature of our coal development. We could not, in all human probability, have reached the development we have attained to-day under the existing regulations. There had to be in the beginning the element of speculation, but it seems to me that we have now reached a reasonable measure of development, and the spirit of speculation having absolutely run wild, it was thought the proper time to put the industry on a basis of development rather than of speculation.
I submit that, with the provision for an extension of the lease on the conditions being fulfilled, the present regulations are more favourable for actual operation than the former ones. The fact that a number of operating mines have taken out leaseholds under the regulations is fair evidence on that point. But to clinch the matter absolutely, the former regulations provided for the sale of the lands and coal area at $10 per acre, subject to a royalty of ten cents per ton. The present regulations provide for the sale of the land-if you like to call it so-at $21 per acre and a payment of royalty of 5 cents per ton.
Now, if you calculate the amount of coal contained in an acre of ground and figure it at 5 cents a ton, you will find, in operation, the land that was purchased at $10 an acre has, in many cases, cost vastly more than that which is leased.
But in one case they own it and in the other they do not.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Precisely-in one case
they do not have to operate it and in the other case they do. 'Consequently, the element of speculation was very pronounced under the former regulations-though, as I have said, those regulations were prefectly proper up to a certain point. That element of speculation was too strong to be allowed to continue in the present condition of the country and especially in view of the fact instanced by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Galliher) that there had been already alienated some of the best areas of coal-bearing lands in the grants to the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Calgary and Edmonton Railway, and the homestead lands given to settlers before the imposition of the royalty. And the fact that we were selling coal lands on a royalty of 10 cents per ton alongside lands that carried no royalty kept out of operation the land that we were selling. We have reduced the royalty by half so that there is only 5 cents a ton between the coal mined under our regulations and coal mined free of royalty. Therefore, there is not the same bar to the operation of coal lands held under our present law as there was under the system of purchase which prevailed before.
Has the minister come to a settlement with the companies in the Crow's Nest Pass that have applied for a rebate ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The companies operating in the Crow's Nest Pass have applied for a rebate or remission of royalty, but so far, we have not been able to give either, and they are required to pay the royalty according to the terms of their purchases.

First, I would like to ask one or two questions in connection with section 10, 17, 17 west of the 4th meridian, concerning which I have been trying to get information for a client of mine in Winnipeg. On June 1, I asked the following question :
1.	When and to whom was patent granted for section 10, 17, 17 west of the fourth meridian?
To this the hon. minister replied:
1. Homestead entry has been granted for the four quarters of this section, but no patent has yet been given for the surface rights to any of the four homesteaders.
As I understand it-I am not well acquainted with these mineral districts-the

surface rights of a given area may be granted to one party and the mineral rights to another, in that case, what protection has the man owning the homestead right against the man who has the mineral rights?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The homesteader owns the surface, but the man who acquires the mineral right, if 'he is operating his coal lands, has rights, practically, of expropriation against the surface holder.

I understand that these parties made application to homestead. It is the second part of the question and its answer that I particularly cannot understand. The question was :
2.	How many applicants were there, what were the names of the applicants, and what was the date of each application?
And the answer of the hon. minister was:
2. No patent has yet been granted for the mineral rights under the section in question, hut there have been five applicants for these mineral rights.
Then follow the names of the five applicants. Now, does the minister mean by this answer that the mineral rights have not been disposed of ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no intimate knowledge of the instance to which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Schaffner) refers, but judging from what he has read I should say that the mineral rights had not been disposed of.
That is what I took from the answer, and sent off that information to my client in Winnipeg. But he was not satisfied; and, on going to the department, I found that these rights had been disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Let me revise the answer. I understood the hon. member to read a direct question asking if the rights had been patented. The question was how many people had applied. The answer did not convey the information that none of these applications had been granted.

However, I find that the mineral rights have been disposed of. Perhaps, I misunderstood it, but I gathered that these rights had not been disposed of at the time I asked the question. But, from information I get, I understand that they were disposed of on March 20, 1907.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Disposed of to one of the applicants named ?

To two of the applicants named. But my client seems not satisfied that these were disposed of at the time his application came in. However, the point is the patent had not been granted, but two applicants had rights on two halfsections, though apparently the patents had not been granted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have not completely paid for it, and therefore they have not got the patent yet.

I asked a question the other night with reference to this Turtle mountain timber reserve, and the minister was not in a position to answer at the time, but said he would refer to it on the next occasion the matter came up. Has he now the information in regard to the resurvey of the land there ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The townships in two ranges, 20 and 21, were subdivided in 1879. The lines were marked with wooden posts, and the marks are now obliterated. A resurvey of these townships has been asked for several times. As most of the lands have been patented and have passed out of the control of the Crown, it was not considered to be the duty of the government to take care of the boundaries. But a resurvey can be undertaken when all the owners or persons having interest in that land shall agree to accept the new .survey and abide by it. Should such an agreement be obtained, the request for a resurvey will receive careful consideration. The land having passed out of our hands we claim that we are relieved from the duty of making a resurvey. A survey made by us now would not affect the rights of the patentees unless they gave their consent. Therefore, while we are willing to go on and make a resurvey, it is absolutely necessary, in order that it may be of any value, that we first get an agreement by the patentees to accept that survey.

I think that is satisfactory as far as it goes. But I think I asked, about two years ago, if a part of this had not been resurveyed. I am told by the settlers that about two years ago a part was resurveyed and iron stakes were put down, but the work was not completed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My information is that the question was asked of the Surveyor General, and he says the request had been made, but that no resurvey had been given.

In regard to the timber reserves in these two townships to which we have been referring, I understood the minister to say that the forest rangers made no report directly to the government, but they made a report to the inspector, and he reported to the government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is as regards the fire rangers, men who are in the transient employment of the government, in the wooded country. But I think that the men who are employed regularly within the forest reserves do report to the head office.
Mr. SCHAFFNER, In the Turtle mountain reserve, for instance, there is one forest ranger who is permanently employed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He would report direct to Ottawa ; but the men whom he employs, would not.
Has he any other du* ties outside those of forest ranger? I refer to Mr. Charles Wakinshaw, forest ranger of the Turtle mountain reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My impression is that he is assigned to the duty of looking after the timber and the general interest of the forest reserve.

What the minister said a few moments ago in reference to reforestation bears out the principle I have been contending for in this House for two or three sessions. I fully recognize the necessity of reserving these forests, if we can do anything with them in view of our climatic conditions. The minister said that after the timber was cut on these so-called reserves it was not always advisable to replant them. I agree with that. I have brought this matter up several times, and more particularly in connection with this very reserve, that part of it which is in township 1, range 21, west of the 1st meridian. That is an illustration of what the minister has been saying. We have a forest there in township 1, range 21, over which the fire swept some years ago, and the timber on it has been practically all destroyed. I stated the other day that all the new timber, trees two, or three, or four years old, in this whole township, could be put into two sections, that would be only two sections out of thirty-six. I took pains to drive over that township last fall, and I say that it has all grown up with grass ; and as I stated the other day, no one knows better than the present Minister of the Interior that trees and grass cannot be grown together. Quite a lot of that land has been cultivated by so-called squatters, though I believe they are now practically all off. But I am confident we can never make a success of growing ti'ees in that particular township. Now the township east of that, which would be township 1 in range 20, I think can be made a success as a forest reserve, but I am confident that township 1 in range 21 cannot be made a success. I agree with the minister that this is a township which comes under his definition, it Is a township that will be useful as farming land. The best of wheat can be grown in the greater part of that township. I have asked before that some inspection be made of that township, because I think it is useless for us to plant trees upon it. Some men have planted trees this year, but they have sown seed on only a limited area of that land which has been cultivated. But undoubtedly seed that was sown on that land which was cultivated last year would grow, because we have had heavy rains. I am talking of the general principle of planting and I would like if the minister
would look into the conditions prevailing in that township. If I am wrong I am willing to take back anything I have said. If we can get timber to grow there that is what we want. However, these settlers are confident that the efforts to establish a timber reserve in that particular township will be a failure and if it will not make a timber reserve they think that these squatters should have their rights recognized. If in two or three years my opinion with regard to the township prevails and this land is open to homesteading, and I have no doubt [DOT]in my mind that it will be, then, I say, that a moral if not a legal injustice will be done to those who have been there for quite a number of years. These men have met with great hardship during the last winter and I do not think it is out of place to make a short statement in connection with that matter. They were promised land away up in the north some place, a great many of them went away last fall and I understand they had a very hard winter. I had a letter with regard to the matter this week. Certain privileges were offered them, they were to get hay and other provision was to be made for them and I understand that some of them have not been very well treated. Although these men had no right to squat on that land they did so and were there for a number of years. They erected buildings and cultivated the land. They were ordered off last fall and perhaps rightly, but if that land is thrown open these men should know it as early as possible and they should receive due consideration. I would like very much that the matter should be looked into by the Minister of the Interior this summer. I do not see why we should not have a proper inspection made. Who is the inspector over Mr. Wakinshaw-Mr. Stevens ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Knechtel, a Canadian by birth who has had experience in scientific forestry in the United States, is the superior officer in the west of the forest rangers who are employed directly on the timber reserves and we depend upon his report from actual examination for final action in regard to these reserves.
Does he live in Winnipeg ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: His headquarters are in Winnipeg.	,
How long has he been in the employ of the government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He came into the employ of the government on the 1st March, 1908, and went west immediately.
Can he have authority to inspect this township ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I propose that he shall make a very careful inspection of the Tur-

tie Mountain reserve. His first orders were to deal with these squatters who had been removed and see that the promises made to them were carried out. I have had some communication which would lead me to believe that he has done so and that the conditions are much more satisfactory than they were formerly.
I do not say that is not possible. Will he make an inspection this summer to determine whether it is suitable for a forest reserve or not

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will certainly assure my hon. friend that it will be inspected by Mr. Ivnechtel. I could not say definitely that a determination will be reached because such a question might depend upon more than the present appearance of the locality. It might require some little time to reach a conclusion.
If that township is inspected and it is determined that it shall be opened to homesteading will these people be reinstated or will they receive any consideration ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that is looking pretty far ahead. These gentlemen had no legal right upon the land, they squatted on that land which was under departmental occupation, they were, under the authority of parliament, required to be removed and we gave them as much consideration as we could in their removal. They have taken land under ordinary homestead right elsewhere and I do not see that they would have any prior right should the township be reopened for settlement at a later date.

They have not all taken up homesteads in another place. Some have gone up there but the land did not suit them as well as in the Turtle mountains and they have not taken up homesteads. I think it would be only fair that these men who spent several years on these lands and made improvements there should be reinstated.

I wish to make a few remarks with regard to the granting of the townsite of Buchanan on the Canadian Northern Railway. The papers in connection with this matter were brought before the Public Accounts Committee and after several attempts I managed to see them while they were in charge of an official of the department. But, I was only able to glance through them very quickly as the official was anxious to get away. I would like to give to the committee the result of the few notes I was able to make and to ask the minister if he will give an explanation of some of the points which stand forth in regard to this question. The townsite is in one of the odd numbered sections which was included in the Doukhobor reserve. It is the northwest quarter of section 35-31-6 west 2nd meridian. At the time that the Mr. OLIVER.
correspondence opened the land was in the possession of Dimitry Soochochen, a Doukhobor, who was the owner of the quarter-section in the early part of 1905. The first matter of interest in the file is a communication from the agent at York-ton on the 29th June, 1905, forwarding Dimitry Soochoehen's abandonment of the north west quarter. I made inquiry in this House as to whether Soochochen had received any consideration for the abandonment and I was given the answer by the minister that he had not. Now, the information comes to me that he did receive a very considerable consideration, that is to say that he got the title to another quarter-section, or rather the title to another quarter-section was vested in Peter Veregin, head of the Doukhobor community, but of this I cannot speak with certainty. On receipt of this communication from the agent at Yorkton, dated 29th June, a telegram was sent by the Commissioner of Dominion Lands to the agent at Yorkton dated 5th July, 1905, as follows :
Dimitry Soochochen has abandoned northwest quarter of section 35; allow O. Ramsland to apply scrip forty acres and homestead balance.
No correspondence appears on the file to show how Ramsland came to be an applicant for this quarter-section, but apparently a week or so after the abandonment had been made a telegram is sent to the agent at Yorkton to allow a certain specified individual to make an entry for a quarter section, partly as a homestead and partly as scrip. This is an odd-numbered quarter-section. I understood the minister the other day to say that when the Doukhobor reservations were thrown open the odd-numbered quarter-sections included were considered in the light of homestead land and were thrown open to homestead entry. Apparently that was done in this case, but it seems to me that one principle at any rate was violated, that after an abandonment had been made of the land, instructions should be sent to allow a particular individual to make an entry on that land. I understood that the rule of the department was that the first applicant should have the first right of entry.
On July 27, the agent at Yorkton wrote asking what portion Ramsland should be allowed to scrip. He went on to explain that he understood that the Canadian Northern Railway had located the townsite of Buchanan on the section and he asked to be advised if the area of the townsite and the right of way was to be reserved and if so he wanted the area defined.	,
The next letter appeared to be after some considrabie delay from the secretary of the Department of the Interior to the agent at Yorkton, dated October 13. He said :
It appears A. J. Sinclair (half-breed) allows to scrip south half. Please report all facts.

Have you ascertained where townsite is located ?
It seems to me that throughout this whole question a good deal must have been done by personal communication, because there are several gaps and no letters appear to take up the continuity of the negotiations.
Next comes an acknowledgment of the abandonment by this Doukhobor, which is returned to the department undelivered, and the right to make a second entry which was sent to I). Soochochen. Apparently neither of them reached him, at any rate the papers were returned uncalled for and appear still on the file. If my information is correct, however, the Doukhobor had not much cause for complaint in this case ; he got other land and apparently handed on the title to the head of the community.
On November 2, 1905, the agent at York-ton informs the secretary of the Department of the Interior that Mr. O. Ramsland made homestead entry for the north half of the northwest quarter, on the 5th of August. He goes on to state that his information with reference to the townsite of Buchanan is that the township is not yet surveyed and when surveyed the entire site becomes the property of Mr. Ramsland according to arrangement with the Saskatchewan Valley Band Company.
The secretary of the Department of the Interior apparently wrote Ramsland on December 22, with reference to a letter which he' had sent to the Minister of the Interior, referred to specifically, and which is not on the file :
It is assumed since the scrip was located thereon that the townsite of Buchanan forms part of the south half of the northwest quarter of 35, which has been assigned to you. There could not have been any, objection on the part of the department to half-breed scrip being located on 80 acres instead of the legal subdivision only.
So it appears that the half-breed scrip finally is located on the whole quarter-section. The patent apparently had issued to Ramsland for the whole section, less right of way and station ground. That is in February, 1906. Ramsland abandons some months later the entry to the north half of this quarter-section in order that he may apply scrip to it and take up another homestead of 160 acres.
The secretary of the Interior on May 11, acknowledges Mr. Ransland's last letter and says :
It has been decided to permit you to scrip this land. This will exhaust your homestead right.
Now apparently he is told that he may take this choice between the two courses, either to scrip the whole of the land and exhaust his homestead right or to continue to homestead the portion for which he had obtained homestead entry. Then apparently some one else steps in and protests 320
against this arranged infringment of Rams-land's right to make another homestead entry.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, when you left the chair I was discussing the question of the town site of Buchanan, and I was referring to the fact that after Mr. Ramsland had been granted the right to place scrip upon the quarter-section upon which the town site was situated, he made a complaint that he was not to be allowed to exercise his right of homestead entry subsequently. I see by the correspondence that apparently Dr. Cash, M.P., the member for that district, complained of the action of the department in informing Mr. Ramsland that in placing scrip upon the quarter-section he had exhausted his right to homestead entry, and that instructions were sent to the land agent at Yorkton by the Commissioner of Dominion Lands that it had been decided that Mr. Ramsland's right of homesteading again had not been exhausted. It [DOT]appears that a little previous to this many of the Doukhobor entries had been cancelled, and that the department had decided that the other three-quarters of this section should be put up for sale at public auction. Instructions were sent to the agent at Yorkton to this effect, with a poster advertising these other three quarter-sections for sale at public auction, and the agent was instructed to give notice that these quarter-sections adjoined the townsite of Buchanan. The instructions went up on May 13. 1907; the sale was to take place on July 8, 1907; but we find that on July 6, there was an application from Mr. Robert Buchanan, a very leading Liberal, I believe, in that district, to purchase one of the quarter-sections. This was granted to Mr. Buchanan, subject to the right of the Doukhobors in tlie property, and there is a memorandum by the chief clerk, dated November 14, 1907, stating that the land was sold to Mr. Buchanan subject to homestead duties. It does not appear in the return what Mr. Buchanan gave for the land. The return does not state that both of the other quarter-sections were put up for sale at public auction; but one of them apparently was sold at public auction for $19 an acre ; and the gentleman who purchased it, Mr. Edward Pinkerton, had in addition to give free right to the Doukhobors to take off their crop and to pay for their improvements. There were eighty acres broken, and he had to pay $2 an acre for this. So that this very desirable quarter-section cost him $20 an acre. The papers are very incomplete. A good deal of the correspondence must have been done privately or the communications may have been personal. At any rate,



this is the way the matter stands: That the government, in possession of the fact that the northwest quarter of section 35, township 37, range 6, west of the 2nd meridian, was destined to be the townsite of the town of Buchanan on the Canadian Northern Railway, agreed, on the Doukhobor who at that time had the homestead right abandoning his homestead, to allow Mr. M. O. Ram-sland to place scrip on the quarter-section and in that way become its possessor; that subsequently, after the cancellation of the homestead entries for the other three-quarters of that section, the government decided to have them put up for sale at public auction; that one of those quarters at any rate was sold privately prior to the public auction to a supporter of theirs, the price not being stated, but carrying with it the homestead duty, so that it may be taken! for granted that the price was not very large. A return has been brought down showing the sales of land during the last year and up to the early part of the present year, and in that return the sale at auction to Pinkerton at $19 per acre does appear, but the sale to Mr. Buchanan of the other quarter-section, with homestead duties attached, does not appear, so that I do not know at what price it was sold to him. At any rate, the whole transaction appears to me to be a very unusual one. and I think the Minister of the Interior should give us an explanation of it-in the first place, why he allowed an odd-numbered section to be taken from the Doukhobor reserve and seripped, and why afterwards he allowed a private sale of a quarter-section to take place just in advance of the sale by public auction, and at a very much smaller figure than it was afterwards found could have been got.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In regard to the townsite of Buchanan, as the transactions occurred some time ago, they are not very fresh in my memory. But, as I gather from what my hon. friend has said and after hurriedly looking through the papers
I informed the Commissioner of Dominion Lands this morning that I was going to bring up the matter, and I was in hopes that he would have the papers here.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have the papers here. As I said, in speaking the other day in regard to the Doukhobor reserves, the Canadian Northern Railway line runs through what was originally the Doukhobor reserve, and in this case runs through a quarter-section that was entered as a homestead of a Doukhobor. At the time the transaction spoken of took place, in the summer of 1905, we had not arrived at any conclusion as to how we were going to deal with the Doukhobor lands; Those who were in this House at the time will remember that when the estimates of that year were under dis-Mr. LAKE.
cussion, some questions were raised, and I think it was made abundantly clear that the department had very little knowledge of the situation with regard to the Doukho-bors. While the information of the department was in that condition and before we had arrived at any conclusion as to how we should deal with the question, it was brought to our attention that the Canadian Northern Railway desired very much to place a station upon this particular quarter-section.
And, if the station were to be placed there, it is altogether desirable, in the interest of the surrounding country, that the land, or a portion of the land, should be available for townsite purposes. My hon. friend will understand that a station of itself is not of the full value that a station is when accompanied with the advantages of civilization and settlement which naturally arise in the vicinity of a station. Therefore, it seemed to us that it was in the public interest that the wishes of the railway company and of the settlement should be met by arranging that this land should become a townsite. Now, it was impossible, as I understand it, to make any arrangement with the Doukhobor who bad entered in regard to this townsite. His entry stood in the books, and it might have been possible to cancel it under the law as it stood. But I did not feel that we were justified in taking action in regard to these Doukhobor entries by piecemeal. I wanted to decide on some policy before I took action in regard to it, and I was not then in a position to decide upon a policy. Therefore, it seemed to me, when the proposition was made that this Doukhobor should be induced to abandon his entry and another man be allowed to take entry of the land-the other man one who would make arrangements in regard to the town-site-that the country stood to lose nothing, because the land was already entered by the Doukhobor, and he was in a position to exercise his rights of proprietorship, for it seemed to me it would not be well, as a matter of sound public policy, to abrogate these Tights at the time. It was a case in which it was better for all parties that a quiet solution should be arrived at. Therefore, the Doukhobor was allowed to abandon his entry and Ramsland, as the first applicant, was allowed to place scrip on part of it and enter as a homestead for the balance. Now, the reason for the permission being given to place scrip on one part and homestead entry on the other was that Ramsland entering upon the whole of the land as a homestead would be in no better position than the Doukhobor to have the land dealt with as a town site, but if he entered three-quarters as a homestead and placed scrip on one-quarter, if he sacrificed his homestead right for 120 acres and placed scrip on the other 40, he would be

in a position to demand a patent for the 40 acres and to place land on the market for townsite purposes. It was with that in view that Ramsland, being the first applicant after the Doukhobor had abandoned the homestead entry, was given the privilege of putting scrip on a part of it in order that it might be used as a townsite, to the advantage as we believe of the railway company and of the surrounding settlement. As is known, the scrip is issued in 240-acre lots-that is, 160 acres and 80 acres. Therefore, we allowed Ramsland to put scrip oh 80 acres instead of 40 as originally intended and to homestead the other 80 acres, and a patent was given him, I presume, for the 80 acres placed under scrip. Ramsland was then in the position that he had 80 acres of land under patent and 80 acres under homestead entry. It is true we could have held Ramsland to the position, but I do not know* that it would be any particular advantage to the country or any one else to retain him in that position, and, as my hon. friend has said, he was given an opportunity to place scrip on the remaining part and was told, as my hon. friend said, he would thereby exhaust his homestead entry. However, up to that time, we had not arrived at a general policy in dealing with the question of placing scrip upon lands that had been homesteaded'. There were cases when it had been permitted and the homestead right had not been exhausted, and there were cases where it had been permitted and the homestead right had been exhausted. It was represented-il assume, as I have not had time to study the matter-that, for one reason or another, Ramsland was entitled to the best treatment, that is to the right of placing scrip upon the land and not exhausting his homestead right. At any rate, that is the treatment that was accorded him. He was given notice, some time in May, I think, that if he placed scrip on the remaining 80 acres he would thereby exhaust his right. But, on June 1 he was notified that he would be permitted to take homestead elsewhere and that the exhaustion of his homestead right would not be insisted upon.
Why was that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not able to answer that question. I have already explained that decision as to exhaustion of the homestead right had depended upon the circumstances of each case. But, shortly after this, we got out our general regulations for the guidance of the department-something that had never been done before, and, under these regulations, we provided that whenever scrip was permitted to be placed upon a homestead, the homesteader's right was thereby exhausted. We have held to that principle, but, up to that time, we had not established that as a principle. I am 320i
assuming that there were circumstances- or there were, in our estimation circumstances-in this transaction of Ramsland's to entitle him to consideration to that extent.
