The minister has not made any explanation of the sale in advance of the public auction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I beg pardon. I am not able to give any explanation to that instance. In the return placed before the House, I think last session, a statement is given of the sales that were made, and this return states specifically that the three quarter-sections in question were sold at auction and the prices are given. I am bound to assume that my hon. friend's statement is correct and that the return is incorrect
Does the minister's file, show that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The file does not sho\w that it was sold at private sale but that it was applied for by Buchanan and that he finally purchased it. The return given to me shows that the three-quarters were sold at public auction.
I was present at the sale and the three-quarters were sold at public auction to the highest bidder. One was bid by Mr. Buchanan and Mr. Ramsland was bidding against him.

What price t
Mr. -CASH. One-quarter sold at $17 the other at $5, and the other, at a price between the two, about $10 or $12.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The figures I have here are $19, $17 and $5 respectively, sold at public auction.
How can the minister account for the fact that in the return brought down, Buchanan's name does not appear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Which return ?
Return No. 88-R brought down the 21st April last.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that. The file does not show that the land was sold to Buchanan at private sale. It shows that he applied for certain lands and got them but does not say that he got them at private sale.
In the papers there is a memo, by the chief clerk ' land sold to Buchanan subject to homestead duties.'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These three sales were all sold subject to homestead duties.

The minister does not seem to have made an explanation which satisfies himself, on account of his not being familiar with the file. He should take

the first opportunity of making a thorough explanation to the House.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of which part ?
That townsite sale.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I suppose it will be agreed that the question of the distribution of the three quarter sections has been settled.

I do not see a complete explanation as to why you told Ramsland that If he scripped eighty acres he would exhaust his homestead rights, and afterwards on June 1, you notified him he would have his homestead rights. The minister said there must be circumstances but did not know what they were. We should have that explained. As to the sale to Buchanan two days before the auction, that ought to be explained.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Cash) has settled that point. He says he was present and saw these three quarter sections sold at auction to the highest bidder, subject to the performance of the settlement duties, and that is in accord with the printed report I have laid on the table.
But the real explanation should come from the papers themselves. The file ought to give a complete explanation, should- it not ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The printed report, which has been before the House ever since the latter part of the last session, says that these sections were sold at auction on the 8th August and that they brought $19, $17, and $5 per acre respectively, realizing a total of $6,453.70.

The application of Mr. Buchanan two days before the sale and the statement in the papers show that my hon. friend from Mackenzie (Mr. Cash) may have been mistaken. The papers left me under the impression that the entry had been granted Buchanan at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In order that we could compel the performance of the homestead duties, the homestead had to be granted.

How is the situation of the Blairmore townsite at present? I have heard it reported that the people residing there are not able to obtain patents for their land. Is the owner able to issue a patent at present or how does it stand ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer at the moment, but I am under the impression that the patent has not yet been issued. There may be some question of adjustment with regard to the grant of land that was to be sub-patented to Pelletier and Lyon.
Another question I want to bring up is the matter of the homestead entries to section 16 of township 24, range 28

west of the second meridian. This is a whole section entered for by a certain Mr. Tanguay and his three sons on the 29th March, 1902. I asked some questions with regard to this particular matter, and the minister will find all that I know about it on pages 3432 and 3433 of ' Hansard.' I asked the minister how many applications there had been for cancellation of two of these homesteads-the two which were held by the sons, namely : the northwest quarter-section and the southeast quarter-section. With regard to the northwest quarter section, the minister said that there had been an application for cancellation on the 19th September, 1903, by W. R. Kane, and that another application had been made on the 4th August, 1906, which the agent had not officially reported. That is to say that the whole number of applications for cancellation with regard to that quarter-section had been two, but that there had been three inspections made by the homestead inspectors of this quarter-section, and that, seven times in succession, extension of time had been given to the holder of the quarter-section.
The date of his entry was the 20th of May, 1902, and extensions were given to him up to the 1st of July, 1907; therefore, for considerably more than five years the land was held for him, although he was not performing the homestead duties. Now,' in regard to the other quarter-section, another son of Mr. Tanguay, Adolphe, made a homestead entry on the 29th of May, 1902. The minister stated that one application for cancellation had been made by W. R. Kane, on the 19th of September, 1903, and that on the 13 th May, 1905, Mr. Robert Brown said that he had applied for an inspection, but this was not officially reportetd. Yet in connection with this same homestead we find that there were three different inspections carried out by officials of the department, that seven distinct extensions of time were given to the applicant to make good his entry ; that he did not put in his residence at all until the 15th of September, 1907, and that after that time permission was given to him to purchase the land. Now the point I wish to make is that there were certain gentlemen applying for cancellation, and that if the persons who had made the entries were not doing their duty, and continued to refuse doing their duty, the persons who had put in the cancellation had the right to get the entry for homestead. I understand that Mr. Brown made an application for the cancellation of both of these homesteads, and he was hoping, up to quite a recent date, to get at any rate the second homestead to which I have referred, that of the southeast quarter-section. I sent to Mr. Brown the answers which the minister had given to my questions in the House, and Mr. Brown stated that they were abso-

lutely incorrect, that his application was still on file, and that he believed that the Mr. Tanguay who held the entry for the southeast quarter had never been a resident. And yet the minister had given permission to have this homestead purchased at $3 an acre, thus depriving Mr. Brown of the right which he undoubtedly had to have that homestead cancelled in his favour. I noticed in some of the correspondence which was sent to me that on the 15th of July 1907, the Hon. Walter Scott, premier of Saskatchewan, w-rote to Mr. Brown in regard to this matter, acknowledging that Mr. Brown and other parties had written to him' about the cancellation of these quarter-sections ; that he was informed that while permission to purchase was cancelled, further extension had been granted the homesteader until the 1st of November following on condition of cultivation and other improvements for the present season. That letter was sent to Mr. Brown. Mr. Scott further informed him that he did not think any good purpose would be served by communicating further about these cases at that time. So Mr. Brown understood that leave of absence had been granted until the 1st of November, and on the 2nd Mr. Brown put in an application for the homestead again. He was met, however, with the statement that the land had already been sold to Mr. Tanguay. I find in the return which was brought down in regard to .the sale of the land that this land was sold to Mr. Adolphe Tanguay on the 21st of October, ten days previously, for $3 an acre, the reason given being that it was his cancelled homestead. Now I would like the Minister of the Interior to give us an explanation of this matter. It seems to me that Mr. Brown had certain rights in regard to this land; it also seems to me that he was done out of these rights, and further, that it is a new departure, according to my idea, that the Minister of the Interior should undertake to sell cancelled homesteads to the persons against whom they were cancelled, especially in cases where, apparently, no residence duty at all had been performed. I would like to ask the minister whether he is prepared to continue these sales of cancelled homesteads in such cases as that, and whether he would make these sales applicable to anybody who chooses to apply for them. It seems to me that the minister must have had very strong reasons to act as he did in this case, and no doubt he will be able to give them to us. I may say further that the following extensions of time were granted to Adolphe Tanguay. It will be remembered that he made his homestead entry on the 29th of Mav 1902 :
Seventeenth November, 1903, until May 1, 1904. On father's representation and promises. April 8, 1904, until May 1. 1905. August 23, 1905, until May 1, 1906; crop destroyed by hail. May 17, 1906, until July 1, 1906; considerable area under cultivation claimed. June 28, 1906, until August 1, 1906. November 12, 1906, until April 1, 1907. May 2, 1907, until November 1, 1907.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not in a position to give the committee full information in this case and I am sure I will be excused from going into the actual details. I have some indistinct remembrance of it, and I am sure my hon. friend will see that in the stupendous number of cases passing through the Interior Department, some proportion of which come to me for final adjustment, I can hardly be expected to keep in mind many of them, at least, so as to be accurate in regard to details. I have a remembrance of the Tanguay case, but I cannot explain it in detail. However, as it comes to my mind, it is something like this : The father and several members of the family went west some time In 1902. The idea was to settle the members of the family together-the father, two or three sons, and, I think, some sons-m-law. It is frequently the case that a father desires to have his sons and sons in-law settled near him. It may have been that, as the practice of accepting proxy entries prevailed at that time, some of the young men did not enter in person and did not go into immediate residence upon their land. I cannot speak upon that point, but, as I remember the case, Tanguay senior and one or two of his sons and sons-in-law did actually settle on land in this neighbourhood, are settled there yet, are settlers who have made substantial improvements were entitled to their patents and have secured their patents. With regard to these two particular quarter-sections, apparently, for one reason or another, the settlement duties were not properly fulfilled, but. on the other hand, I think the evidence is that a substantial amount of work was done upon these homesteads by the father on behalf of these sons, or by the sons themselves. In so far as I can remember, it was represented to me that when these young men had put in some part of their residence duties and very fully complied with the requirements of the law with regard to cultivation, it had become impossible, in the transaction of their business, to actually settle upon that land, and it was a question as to whether they should lose what they had done, that is lose the value and the advantage of their improvements and residence, or whether they should adopt some means of permitting them to acquire title. There have been many cases in which we have done this: When a settler had, to a measurable degree earned his patent, that is to say, when he had completed practically the duties but had not entirely completed the duties, we were not entitled to give him the patent of a free homestead, and yet it would not be fair, in our estimation to deprive him of the time labour and money which he had expended upon the homestead; we have,

in order to clear the account, in fairness both to the government and to the settler, sold him the land. When a settler had resided upon his land to the full requirements of the law, except, It may be, a few days, a week or two, sickness had intervened, he had made a miscalculation, something had occurred, he had fulfilled the duties, except a small portion of the residence duties, we have, in order that we may be able to give that man his patent, in order that he may not lose the time and labour that he has placed upon the land, sold it to him at a dollar an acre. Then again, if he has been short of his residence duties but has performed his cultivation duties to the satisfaction of the department we have sometimes sold to him, in order to square the account, at $3 per acre.
Suppose he has done no residence duties at all?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In that case our practice is not to do anything but to cancel the entry. Our information is that these Tan-guays did perforin their residence duties, not to a sufficient extent to entitle them to their land, but that they did their other duties either themselves or through their father in the way of cultivation and imf provements to such a degree as would, apart j from residence, fully entitle them to their patent. It is on that principle that we have made the sale that my hon. friend mentions and of which Mr. Brown complained. It may be that in this case we have erred by being too liberal in our construction of the practice, but, in administering the lands of the country, in order to secure settlement and development, it has been the practice to give every reasonable consideration to the actual settler who is on the land and especially to the families of settlers. My hon. friend knows that it is a definite provision of the Land Act that if a man has ten sons all may acquire patents for their homesteads without ever living a day upon the land ; but by residing with their father they can complete all the duties upon their homestead. While we refuse proxy entries generally one member of a family may make a proxy entry for the other members of the family. It is considered to be sound public policy to give consideration to the desire of families to settle together and it was in pursuance of that idea that the consideration which we have given to the Tanguays was given to them. Perhaps we erred a little, but we believe we erred on the right side in giving consideration to these people and allowing them to protect the expenditures which had been made on their behalf and retain the land in the neighbourhood in which the other members of their family are located.

I sympathize with the minister in the position which he takes that facilities should be afforded to families to settle together. But, in this particular case, iMr. OLIVER.
apparently one son, to whom permission was given to purchase his homestead, never performed any residence duties at all until a month before the purchase was permitted. The gentleman who brought this matter to my notice apparently is under the impression that the son has never set foot upon the land at all even up to the present time, although the government state that he had gone into residence just a month before permission was given to him to purchase the land. I think it ought to be understood that if proof can be adduced that no residence duties at all have been done in a case of this sort cancellation ought to take place. The minister agrees to that.
Another point is that Mr. Brown says he made application for cancellation of both these quarter-sections at different times. In one case the minister apparently has no record of his application. In the other case he simply states that Mr. Brown says he put in an application but does not know whether that is the case or not.^ These applications for cancellation are important particularly in regard to priority, because if a man knows that the duties are not being performed on a desirable homestead, and believes there is no intention to perform them he has a right to expect that the law will be carried out and unless there is a valid reason that cancellation will take place. In these cases, from the government's own showing, cancellation apparently never took place and the gentleman had to go elsewhere. I have known of other cases where there has been strong feeling in regard to this question of cancellation. 1 have had correspondence with the department in reference to more than one of them. I wish to impress on the minister the absolute necessity of having a complete record of these applications for cancellation because the man who applied for cancellation has rights under the law which should be respected.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the view of my hon. friend in regard to cancellation.	I hope that he and
the House will understand that cancellation is one of the most difficult questions with which we have to deal in the administration of the lands. We have to be guided on one hand by considerations of the rights of the worthy but poor settler, and on the other hand we have to give due consideration to the rights of the man who wants to fulfil the duty which the other man is failing to fulfil. It would be impossible to fulfil the law so as to satisfy both parties when a conflict necessarily exists between the homesteader and the applicant for cancellation. From time to time since June last we have defined our position in regard to cancellation as fully, as completely and we believe, as fairly as has been possible under the very difficult circumstances. I do not know whether my hon. friend is ac-
1Q093

quainted with the regulations in regard to cancellation, but we find that from time to time the healing of one difficulty is followed by the opening of a new difficulty. It is impossible to foresee the ingenuity of man in protecting his entry when it ought not to be protected or in attacking another man's entry when it ought not to be attacked. We can only try to strike a fair average in dealing with these hundreds of cases and we hope to get fair consideration for trying to do what is right and fair between man and man according to the best interests of the settlement of the country. We do not pretend that we are able to please both sides to a dispute in which only one can win.

I have seen a good deal of this question, particularly in my own locality. I can say from experience that I commend the minister for a great many acts of his in the way of being lenient, while still within the law, to settlers in allowing men to purchase in some cases at a dollar an acre, and in some at $3 an acre, if they have not fulfilled all the requirements of the law. But at the same time I know-many cases in my locality where the government has been either very seriously imposed upon by people getting places or else a great deal of partiality has been shown. I know one place near my own town where a man had an entry for a quarter-section. He was not able to go on it for the first six months, but I do not know that he did not get an extension of time for six months. However, before the second term was up he was notified his entry would be cancelled, if he could not show reason why he had not done certain improvements. He was not able to comply with the law and another man got his entry. This man held it about two years. He never resided on it or made any attempt to reside on it, and he was allowed to purchase it at, I think, $3. As soon as he got the patent he sold the land for $20 an acre, but he had never made any attempt to live on the land or improve it. There are a great many other cases of the same kind I have seen. The minister has been lenient and I would recommend him to be lenient with men who have made a conscientious attempt to comply with the conditions.

I wish to ask the minister as to the disposal of the quarantine lands near Estevan. They were disposed of apparently by public auction. What where the conditions of sale, where were they advertised, what time was given to carry them out and what bids were received ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This relates to a certain area of land, about two sections, on the boundary line near Estevan, about where the Soo line crosses the boundary. They were reserved for the use of the Agricultural Department for holding stock in quarantine upon them. After a time the Agricultural Department decided that they did not require them any longer and they were released from reservation, in the meantime the land around had settled up and they had become, as we thought, of some little increased value. We felt that if they were open to ordinary homestead entry there was likely to be a good deal of hard feeling about priority of entry. Therefore in July, 1907, they were put up for sale at an upset price of $3 per acre subject to settlement conditions, that is to say subject to cultivation of twenty acres and 12 months residence. No tender for more than one-quarter section was to be accepted from the same applicant. Tenders were received in the department, but the sale was not carried out in view of an irregularity in regard to the highest tender. The cheque accompanying it was not certified or marked by the bank, in accordance with the conditions of the advertisement. The cheque accompanying the next tender had been marked by the bank, but we did not feel justified in accepting it, although it was really the highest that complied with the terms of the advertisement, as the lack of the mark on the cheque accompanying the highest tender might have been only an inadvertence. Therefore we decided that for the time being we would call the sale off and again advertise the lands for sale by public auction, when no mistake would be likely to occur in regard to the cheque. The date of this sale has not yet been fixed, but it will take place some time during this summer.
What are the sections ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Half of section 6, half of section 16, three-quarters of section 18, and one-quarter of section 23.

The return brought down says that the northeast quarter of section 16 was sold by tender on the 15th of October to James Rutherford at $3 per acre. How did that tender come to be received ? I understood from the minister that the tenders were called for in July.
iMr. OLIVER. The information I have is that the lands were to be put up in July to be sold on the 16th of December. It may have been that the date was postponed from October to December.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The House will see that these lands are for sale, not at the highest price, but under settlement conditions,

which of course detracts considerably from the price that would otherwise be got for them. The statement that $7.50 per acre was offered must be a mistake. It is quite possible that the land would be worth that figure as a speculative proposition, but I do not think we would receive any such figure with settlement conditions attached. However, the sale did not go through, and the land will be offered at public auction some time this summer.

Is it an absolute rule that unless a homesteader literally fulfils the settlement conditions, he cannot get his patent, and that all the government can do in such a case is to allow him to purchase at a certain reasonable price ? Suppose a man did his settlement duties for three years, doing everything that was necessary in the way of building a shack, breaking his land and putting it under crop, but something occurred to make a break in the performance of his residence duties, would he not be able to get his homestead entry ? Is that absolute ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is as we understand it. We have no authority to issue a patent unless the requirements of the statute are fulfilled. There is, however, an instance in which we have stepped outside the statute, and in the proposed amended Land Bill I am asking for provision for that; that is, where ia settler suffers from some physical disability that absolutely incapacitates him from fulfilling his duty. In one or two instances of this kind we have taken an order in council as authority for issuing the patent.

After a man has gone on and done his duty faithfully as a bona fide homesteader, something might happen, like the fall from a load, to prevent him fulfilling all the conditions; and it scarcely seems fair justice to say to him, you can buy your homestead for $3 an acre, when other land can be bought at the same price. There ought to be a remedy somewhere, whether by report to parliament or otherwise. It seems very harsh that the result of three years work should be entirely voided because of some unforeseen and unavoidable accident.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The best we can do in such a case is to sell the land at $1 an acre, unless in a case where the man is absolutely incapacitated and then we get an order in council.
I think you would have to come to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Possibly, but once the patent is issued, I do not think the government is subject to political attack or the patent to a legal attack. I wish to remedy that position by an amendment to the Act, so that there will be no question about the Mr. OLIVER.
authority. The best we can do is to sell at $1 an acre, and we only sell at $1 an acre when there is merely a trifling difference between the performance and the duty.
Is that ministerial administration or by order in council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is ministerial. There is a provision in the Act that the minister may sell at $1 an acre, and he exercises that power in that case. In such a case as that mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelie (Mr. Lake), where we sell at $3 an acre, there has been a substantial failure in the residence, but a liberal fulfilment in the cultivation. We simply say that the man has failed in the essential particular required by the statute, but in order that he may save the money that he has put into the land we make the sale to him.

I notice by the return that in the aggregate there are a large number of those sales at from $1 to $3 an acre and sometimes more than $3. Is that done on ministerial responsibility or is an order in council required?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are dealt with by ministerial authority. In the few instances where the price is over $3 the sales are in British Columbia.
Are there any sales at $2 an acre?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There may have been, but since I have been minister we have either made it the one way or the other. They are made at $1 an acre in order to save the man who has substantially fulfilled his residence duties, but we sell at $3 an acre to the man who has failed in what we consider an essential part of his duties, the residence. We do not sell to any one who has altogether failed in his residence duties. There must be some residence or there is no sale. There is another instance where we sell, namely, where there are fractional pieces of land adjoining lakes or large rivers-a piece less than eighty acres, the corner frequently of an adjoining homestead. Our practice is to sell that to the owner of the adjoining land, believing that the area is too small to warrant any one taking it as a homestead and believing that, if the adjoining owner wants it it is reasonable he should have it, and we sell it at that price.

The minister must be, to a large extent, at the mercy of his officials who report to him from all through the country. Does he think that these officials are influenced by political or party considerations? Some of these difficulties may arise from that fact.	.
Mr. OLIVER, By the time the case comes from the inspector to the agent and from the agent to the head office and runs the gauntlet in the head office, it is pretty

well trimmed of anything but its merits, and there is not much chance to hang anything else to it.
What is Mr. Obed Smith's position now?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is assistant immigration commissioner in London, England.
Is he there permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As permanent as anything in the outside service. An exchange was made early this spring between Mr. J. Bruce Walker, who was assistant immigration commissioner in London, and Mr. Smith, who was assistant commissioner in Winnipeg. The salary was the same in both cases.

Does the minister issue instructions to his land officers throughout the west, by circular or otherwise, forbidding them to engage in the business of buying and selling land or changing or otherwise the homesteads?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think there is a provision in the Land Act itself which forbids an employee of the Lands Department from taking part in any transactions having relation to government land. It does not forbid their engaging in transactions with regard to other lands. I do not know that we have issued any instructions, but the Land Act is very definite.
I notice that a number of pieces of land have been sold to the Grand Trunk Pacific for townsite purposes at $1 an acre. Does the minister consider that a proper price?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The land was sold to the homesteader at $1 an acre and he sells to the company for whatever he can get. The Grand Trunk Pacific of course runs through lands owned by private individuals and other corporations as well as through government lands, and it is necessary that they should not only have stations but conveniences for the handling of grain and other business in order that they may give full benefit and advantage to the surrounding country. In placing their stations where they will be most suitable the company frequently has to select quarter-sections occupied by homesteaders. The homesteaders could not sell that land to the Grand Trunk Pacific and could not make it into a town-site, and it amounted to a hold up of the development of the town at that particular place until he got his patent.
Where the settler got his patent he would do as he pleased with it. Under these circumstances, the railway company, being desirous of getting action for the development of this town as soon as possible, for the sake of the business, and for the sake of knowing definitely where they were, desired to acquire these lands. Now, so far1
as the government was concerned, the right to the land had already passed, and there was no way by which the government could recover its ownership in that quarer-section. The homesteader had the right to earn the title, and, so far as we knew, he woukb earn it and would become the owner. Therefore, it was a mere question of allowing the railway company to get beneficial action upon the property or delaying that action until the homesteader earned his patent. In order that action might be had as soon as possible, we sold the land that the railway company wanted to purchase for a townsite to the homesteader and he sold to the railway company for what he could get. I hope he made a g"ood sale. We allowed him to take land elsewhere. It was a fortunate thing for the homesteader, and, I say frankly. I do not regret giving him the advantage, for the government lost nothing and it was not a matter of taking advantage on the part of the homesteader. He was there as a settler, the railway came and made his land valuable in spite of him, and I know no reason why he should n'ot get the benefit. Where the railway saw fit to place its station upon land still remaining in the Crown, the arrangement is different. There we think it quite fair and reasonable that there should be facilities for the establishment of a town, and we sell the land to the company at $3 an acre, retaining one-quarter interest in the proceeds of the sales that may be made. The reason why we prefer to retain an undivided one-quarter interest is that if we were to retain a divided interest the question of municipal taxation would necessarily arise, and we have found that a very difficult and vexing question. It Is a generally established principle that the government pays no taxes. We do not feel that we should be warranted in breaking through that rule and paying taxes on the land when it became part of the municipality. Therefore we conclude that probably the best way to deal with the matter was to sell the land to the railway company at a price and simply retain an interest in whatever result might Come from the future sales. I think the transaction is one that will commend itself to the House and the country.
But if you had braved the dangers of municipal taxation, your relation with the railway company would be that you would have one-lialf the townsite still.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That would be the usual system of dealing with a railway company.
Instead of that, you keep one-quarter upon which you pay no taxation. That is, you keep the municipality out of the taxation

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is
Well, you cut them oul of it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, the railway company owns tlie land and has to pay taxes.
On the whole 'of it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. If it were divided, part of it would not pay taxes.
The minister says that the government charge $3 an acre, but the return shows that the amount paid is $1 per acre. That is why I asked the question, thinking $1 too low a price.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The mistake must arise in the case of townsites where the purchase is made by the homesteader.
It does not show that in the return.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am satisfied that that is how it arises. When we sell to the homesteader we sell at $1 an acre, but when we sell to the company we sell at $3.

In this return, wherever the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite and Development Company is mentioned, the price is $1 an acre, and I see no sale at $3 an acre. Sales should appear in the return as they were made? Another question I would like to ask the minister is in reference to one sale by G. II. McKague, 160 acres at $2.50 per acre ' in lieu of cancelled pre-emption.' What is the explanation of that?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot recall the particular point mentioned. But I may say that the question of pre-emptions is one that arises occasionally. The right of pre-emption expired some time about 1889. But, though it is so long ago since this right expired, there are isolated cases where the pre-emption patent has not yet been issued because of the failure of the homsteader to complete his payment for pre-emption or for some other reason. It may be that there is some part of the payment due, or it may be that there is a seed-grain lien, or a lien of some other kind against the land. In any case, every now and again, we come across a pre-emption entry of which the homesteader is not entitled to a patent and the question arises what we are to do with it. In some cases, they have paid part of the price, and it seems hard that the man should lose what he has paid, even though he has not entirely completed the payment. I do not recall the instance my hon. friend has mentioned, but I can imagine that it was of this character. We find in our books an instance of pre-emption the payment upon which had not been completed, and not being able to get into communication with the homesteader or the man who had the preemption we have cancelled it. After a time, the owner has waked up and found that he has lost some property. He comes to us with his tale of woe; he tells us that he paid part of the money and could have paid the balance if he had known, that he Mr. FOSTER.
ought to have it, that we ought not to rob him, and so on. And it may be that we have felt there was merit in the man's ease and have met his grievance in the way my hon. friend suggests. I do not know that this is such a case, but I say it is quite possible it may arise in that way. The other day a case came before me where a pre-emption owner had notice that his preemption was cancelled. Though he had got it in 1889, and had paid $240 out of $480, he had never been able to raise the balance, and it was only when he got notice that his land was cancelled that he woke up and came back to us, and wanted reinstatement and the privilege of paying up the balance of the price.

I would like to mention another matter that has created a good deal of feeling in the neighbourhood where I have been living. There have been complaints that certain parties are able to get cancellations in the land office at Regina when other parties cannot do so. It is also complained that the government officials are in the habit of taking money from settlers, and giving cancellations which other parties were not able to procure. This was brought to my notice some time last year, and I think I called the attention to it of the Commissioner of Dominion Lands. Later on when I got home, it was again called to my attention. Several different individuals came to see me about it, and told me of case after case. I was not able to go into these eases and verify them. But something did happen which enables me to bring the matter before the minister. I will not give the names, because I do not know if the complaints are well founded ; but the minister will easily be able to identify the case which I propose to lay before him. A certain individual stated that he had been approached by one of these parties who professed to be able to control the cancellations, and had offered to get the cancellation of a certain very desirable quarter-section on payment of the sum of $400. I may say that he was a supporter of hon. gentlemen opposite. This individual went to the land office and found that he could not get a cancellation. But he there and then made an affidavit, which was taken in the land office, and I will read the affidavit, leaving out the names. I think the minister will agree that it is just as well the names should not be mentioned :
I .... do solemnly declare that the homesteader is not in residence, and has made no improvements. The only improvement on the place is thirty acres broken in 1905 by a party at	who told me last year that he
could let me have this land for $200. The land was entered for on October 17 last, and the entrant has not started to live on it, but states that he can let me have it for $400. I understand that he has written to have it protected.

The matter was reported to the head office here, and the homestead inspector was told to report. His report states:
I have not discovered any evidence of manipulation in connection with the evidence.
I cannot believe that the homestead inspector could have made the inquiry he ought to have made under the circumstances, because I know from the amount of talk all through the neighbourhood, that he must have been able to get something more than is contained in that report. I would like the minister to make inquiry and see whether there is any ground for this complaint. It is in connection with this same office that I mentioned, as furnishing complaints about cancellations not having been properly recorded.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not able to follow the incidents my hon. friend has mentioned. Certainly, the idea that there is favouritism in cancellations is very injurious to the standing of the department in the minds of the public, and is therefore an injury to the settlement of the country, because confidence in the administration of the land office must lie at the foundation of successful settlement. It has been my object to establish that confidence. Our departmental regulations in regard to cancellation read as follows :	[DOT]
Application for the cancellation of the entry of a homesteader in default, must be made in person at the land agency for the district within which the land is situated.
How long has that been in force ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say how long it has been in force, but it has been printed and in the hands of all parties concerned ever since the 1st of October last.
That is subsequent to a good many of the cases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then it goes on, a page and a half of provisions intended to guard against fraudulent applications for cancellation. There was, as we found some years ago, a great abuse in the matter of cancel-lationg. There was no restriction, anybody could go into a land office and apply for a cancellation of a whole township for homestead entry. Among some of the other provisions of these regulations, are the following :
An application for cancellation will not be accepted or considered if made within six months of the date on which the homestead entry was granted, unless the application should be made on the ground of ineligibility of fraud. In such case the application may be accepted at any time after the date of entry, and must be accompanied by a statement on oath giving full particulars.
Only one application for cancellation will be accepted against an entry until such application has been finally disposed of.
The applicant for cancellation must be eligible to make homesteading, except in the case of a minor, and eligible to have land reserved for him.
I am aware that circulation of reports such as those my hon. friend has mentioned are injurious, and I will be glad to follow them out to a finish, if he will furnish me with information. I am afraid there may have been matters that were not absolutely correct in the Regina land office some time ago. As my hon. friend is aware, there was a change of agency there over a year ago, and I was under the impression that matters were more satisfactory since. I am not a respecter of persons, I want to have the confidence of the people with regard to the fair administration of the land laws, and if, on investigation, I find that a wrong has been done, wherever the lightning strikes somebody will be hurt.

I am very glad to be able to bring these matters to the attention of the minister. I have been in communication with respect to two or three of them with the Commissioner of Dominion Lands who, no doubt, will bring them to the attention of the minister. I expect that the commissioner knows about this particular matter to which I have just referred. A return was brought down in connection with it. There is just one other matter to which I desire to call the attention of the minister. I have had several resolutions sent to me by boards of trade in the southern part of my constituency, one of which is as follows :
Resolved, that this board heartily endorses the resolution recently passed by the Saskatchewan Game Protective Association in respect to the establishment of a national park and game preserve in the Moose mountains and the placing therein of a herd of buffalo and other wild game.
Has the minister been able to give any consideration to the question of forming a park in the Moose Mountains ? I see that a good deal has been said about it lately. It is an ideal spot for a timber and game preserve. I would like to hear from him in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the project of purchasing a herd of buffalo in Montana was first brought up the Moose Mountain timber reserve was the place I had in mind for the location of the herd. But, afterwards, when I heard of the resentment that was felt locally against the removal of the herd from Montana, I thought it would be rather doubtful policy to place such a large herd of buffalo within what you might term easy reach of the boundary line.
What would the distance be ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
About forty miles which is not a very long run for a band of buffalo. I thought it would be better to place them

temporarily where they were placed and afterwards make arrangements for an area of grazing land where they would be practically out of reach of anything of that kind. At the same time I am aware of the advantages of the Moose Mountain country and I quite sympathize with the desire of the people to have some specimens of game there. When we get our buffalo settled down, when we get our principal grazing ground entirely inclosed and our herd installed there I will be very glad to take up the question of pleasure parks, as they may be called, in different parts of the country. As my hon. friend is aware, there is an Indian reserve adjoining the forest reserve at Moose Mountain. We have been able to secure from the Indians the surrender of a piece of land adjoining a very pretty lake there with the view of it being used as a summer resort and I think that in due course we may be able to do something in the way that the resolution suggests, but at the present time we do not feel that we are in a position to deal comprehensively and intelligently with the question of the location oi the buffalo beyond what we have already decided. It is an old saying that you must first catch your hare before you can cook him, and I would like to have all the buffalo that we are going to get well in hand before I decide upon the policy of distribution.
How many are there in the herd now ?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are about 400.
iMr. FOSTER. How are they distributed as to sex ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry to say that the majority is against us, b-ut still there is a fair proportion-well, not a fair proportion as breeding cattle are understood-but we have a very considerable number of females and there was some measure of increase this spring although owing to the rough handling last summer there has not been as great an increase as we otherwise might have expected.

As I had some experience of buffaloes in the early days, I have great sympathy with the government in procuring that herd. I think they did well to secure the buffalo which are natives of our land, but I rather think it was unfortunate that they were placed in the northern country where they are at present. Does the government not anticipate a great deal of trouble in securing and removing them from the present place to the new park laid out for them or the place where it is intended to locate them permanently ? I understand that they are in a wooded or partially wooded country. I doubt very much if the government will ever be able to secure the buffalo from that timbered country, get Mr. OLIVER.
them loaded on the cars and move them to another part of the country. You cannot do that with ordinary domestic cattle in a timbered country. It is impossible to get them out of the timber until they are ready to come. I do not know what is to be done with the buffalo. I feel certain that there will be great disappointment in getting them out. Has the government taken that into consideration ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the government has taken it into consideration but it is one of those things which is really not for consideration. It is something that has to be done. I quite appreciate the difficulties of it but I do not see any other recourse and I have no doubt that, when we were able to secure so many of the herd as we did under the unfavourable circumstances which surrounded our getting them, we will be able to make the transfer from the park where they are to the park where we want to keep them permanently.
Are they inclosed at present ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, they are in an inclosure four miles square. As my hon. friend (Mr. Herron) says, part of the area is wooded and part is prairie. It is a very nice location in itself but it is not an ideal buffalo range, but the park which we have now reserved and for the fencing of which we are asking an appropriation, is in a part of the country which is considered to be an ideal buffalo range. We hope to get the park fenced in time to receive the remainder of the herd that we hope to get from Montana this summer and later will make the transfer.

You have 400 already and you expect to get more ?
Mr. OLIVER, It is believed that there are about 200 more. When we entered into the bargain first we thought that the whole herd amounted to 350, but as they were on a wide range and had not been rounded up it was impossible to ascertain the exact number. But we feel that we are getting them at a price at which we can afford to take the whole herd and if we are able to corner the market by getting the whole herd that fact will appreciate the value of what we have.
Mr. FOSTER, You did not buy them by the number ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We got them at so much per head.	.
How much per head ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: $200 per head landed at Edmonton, plus the actual cost of transportation, which amounts to $45 per head. The seller stood the loss until arrival at Edmonton. We paid only for what arrived at Edmonton.
Who negotiated the purchase?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. H. Douglas, superintendent of the park at Banff.
Had he any assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think so, Mr. Ayotte, the immigration agent at Grand Forks, may have assisted in Mr. Douglas' absence.
That gentleman was a deputy returning officer in the last Dominion election in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware.
I saw in a western paper that he had assisted in the purchase and had made a clean up of $25,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no hesitation in saying that as far as the clean up is concerned, the statement is absolutely untrue.
In reference to the purchase of lands by the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, have all these lands been paid for and the patents made out and have the lands become liable to taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that definitely. If the payments have been made the patents will issue without delay.
Are not the patents completed ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I understand so.
And all conditions fulfilled?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That Is our understanding.
How many acres of swamp land were transferred to the Manitoba government this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot give that. I think we have transferred in all about 2,000,000 acres ; about three-quarters of a million acres were transferred this year.
How many acres of Dominion lands are there still in Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say until tomorrow.	*
Who are the inspectors inspecting the swamp lands in Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Dukes and Mr. Ducker are and have been for some years.
What conditions are required to qualify lands as swamp lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The requirement, is set out in an order in council. Roughly it is that some portion, one-quarter or one-half of a quarter-section, must have been at some time under water. Then it can be reported as swamp land and we can transfer it.

The minister knows that it has been a grievance in the province for
many years that according to the Act of 1885 about 7,000,000 acres should have been turned over to the province long before now, and not more than two and a half million or three million acres have been transferred. That land is drying up and what would have qualified as swamp ten years ago would not qualify now. The province is losing a good asset owing to the delay in inspecting and turning over the lands. Before and after the change of government here, Mr. Greenway, then the leader of the provincial government, said that upon the Liberals coming into power in Ottawa these lands would be quickly turned over to the provincial government, but they have not been.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know my hon. friend's authority for the statement that there are 7,000,000 acres which should be transferred to the province.
That was the estimate in 1885.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It may be that in all Manitoba there are 10,000,000 acres that would qualify, but the agreement is that the lands are only to be handed over on their being surveyed. As the survey has progressed the inspection has been made and the lands handed over. We have now handed over 2,000,000 acres and there remains very little that has been inspected and surveyed to be handed over. There is, however, an account to be adjusted between the two governments in respect of lands which have been handed over to the province as swamp lands and which have been squatted upon by settlers before being handed over. In the protection of the rights of these settlers it has been necessary to make some adjustment with the province of Manitoba. This account is still open, but as far as the lands are concerned they are inspected and handed over. The grievance that the province of Manitoba is suffering because lands which were not handed over as swamp lands some years ago have become dry and are now not eligible to be handed over as swamp lands, may be. a good argument on behalf of Manitoba, but I am afraid that my hon. friend will not receive sympathy from other sections of the Dominion in his complaint, because if it was a loss to Manitoba it was a corresponding gain to the Dominion. But I think my hon. friend's contention is imaginary rather than real. Taking one year with another, the average has been about even, and the province does not stand either to lose or gain by delay.

I think the province of Manitoba should have its rights; and should not lose this valuable asset by lapse of time. There has been nothing to prevent this government in the last ten years putting on the necessary surveyors and inspectors to survey these lands, so that they

could have been handed over to the province ; and I am sure that the sister provinces of this Dominion would not consider that Manitoba was getting the best of them. It is generally conceded throughout this Dominion that the province of Manitoba has not been treated as it should have been by this government. I do not think the other provinces want to take an unfair advantage of the province of Manitoba, or make a gain from the fact that these lands, by the lapse of time, are continually drying up and will not qualify as swamp lands. If they had been inspected ten years ago and had been turned over to the province at that time as swamp lands, the province would have got the benefit. I am not making this complaint against this government only, but against the late Conservative government as well. What the people of Manitoba expect is fair treatment, and therefore I would ask the minister to take immediate action to put on the necessary surveyors and inspectors, and turn over to the province what lands will qualify as provincial swamp lands.

In connection with this item I have a matter placed in my hands which I do not understand very well, and I am going to ask the minister to allow us to take it up on some other of his items, so that we may get the information required.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is it in connection with ?

It is in connection with a request of the Robbins Irrigation Company for a re-arrangement of their lands.
Government of the Yukon Territory, $365,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: For salaries and expenses connected with the administration of the territory $165,000 was voted for the fiscal year 1907-8, and the same amount is asked for the current fiscal year. The principal items are: salaries, $70,720; living allowances, $40,800; insane patients' expenses connected with transportation to asylum at New Westminster and for maintenance at Dawson and Whitehorse. $15,000; travelling expenses to and from Dawson and the territory, $5,000, printing and stationery, $7,000; advertising mining regulations, proclamations, &c., $5,000; telegrams, telephones and postage, $2,500 ; expenses connected with collection of export tax, $3,500; to pay commission of 10 per cent to the Royal Northwest Mounted Police on sums collected by them as mining recorders and inspectors, $6,000.
Is the minister making any change with reference to living allowances ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is no change proposed in these estimates. The living-allowances are the same this year as last, and Mr. STAPLES.
j they were the same last year as the year before.
I understand that Mr. Gi-rouard is no longer registrar, and that some re-arrangement has been made. Will the minister explain what that is ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Girouard has retired, and Mr. LalibertS, who was librarian to the Justice Department, has been made registrar at $3,800 salary and $1,200 living allowance instead of $4,000 salary and $1,500 living allowance which Mr. Girouard received. His salary as librarian of the Jusice Department I understand will drop.
What was that salary ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to answer that, as it is in another department; but the idea is to combine the duties of the two offices under the one salary, which shall be that of the registrar.
It has been charged that there are too many officers there at present for the work there is to do. Has the minister looked into that ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that some time ago there was considerable reduction in the number of officials. I am not able at present, beyond this change with regard to Laliberte, to offer any proposal for reduction. The commissioner of the Yukon was here a little while ago in connection with the reduction that we proposed to make in connection with the government of the Yukon, and I discussed the matter with him, and he informed me that he was not able at the moment to make any suggestion as to reduction. I urged on him the desirability of reductions being made if they could be made, but I regret to say that in one or two instances he seemed to think that more assistance would be heeded rather than less. For instance, he says that the surveys are very much behind, and that we should have more assistance in that work.
What are the duties of F. T. Oongdon, who is receiving a very large salary and a large living allowance 7

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Congdon is not in the employ now. He retired about a year ago. He was legal adviser. When Mr. Congdon retired, Mr. Senkier, who before that was gold commissioner', was made legal adviser at the same salary and with the same living allowance. Mr. Gosselin, who had been assistant gold commissioner, was made commissioner, and the office of assistant was dropped, it being believed that, with The Placer Mining Act, there was not the necessity that formerly existed for a gold commissioner and an assistant.

Has any reduction been made in the number of clerks in the Gold Commissioner's office ? There seems to be

altogether too many of them. For instance you have appointed a clerk, L. G. Bennett, gold commissioner's office, getting a salary and allowance of $1,690 for the. nine months; Bolduc, a clerk, gold commissioner's office, with a salary and allowance of $1,600 for the nine months ; a stenographer, gold commissioner's office, with a salary and allowance of $1,837 for the nine months ; Aime Dugas, a clerk in the gold commissioner's office at $1,900 salary and allowance for the nine months ; Finnic, chief clerk, gold commissioner's office, $2,625, salary and allowance for the nine months ; another mining inspector, and then you have Fysh, clerk, gold commissioner's office, $2,025. salarv and allowance for the nine months ; Gosselin, assistant gold commissioner, with a salary and allowance of $3,900 for the nine months ; Grant, clerk, gold commissioner's office, salary and allowance, $1,800 for the nine months. Then more mining inspectors. Then L'Hereux, clerk, gold commissioner's office, $1,100, salary and allowance for the nine months ; Little, stenographer, gold commissioner's office, $2,025, salary and allowance for the nine months ; Macfarlane, clerk, gold commissioner's office, $1,760, salary and allowance for nine months. Then you have an accountant in the gold commissioner's office at $1,500, salary and allowance for the nine months. Another stenographer and gold clerk, at $2,475, salary and allowance for the nine months. An assistant gold commissioner at White Horse, over $3,000, salary and allowance for the nine months; G. D. Munroe, clerk, gold commissioner's office, salary and allowance. $1,440 for the nine months ; W. O. Noble, clerk, gold commissioner's office, $1,650, salary and allowance for the nine months ; G. Fepin-that is the ministrel, I suppose-clerk, gold commissioner's office, $1,575, salary and living allowance for the nine months ; G. Petre, clerk, gold commissioner's office, salary and living allowance, $1,500 for the nine months ; A. H. Povah, gold commissioner's office, $1,370, salary and living allowance nine months ; E. C. Sinkler, gold commissioner, salary and living allowance for the nine months, $4,875. Another stenographer in the gold commissioner's court, $1,586, salary and living allowance for the nine months : another stenographer, gold commissioner's office, $1,575, salary and living allowance, nine months ; a correspondence clerk, salary and living allowance, $1,800 for the nine months ; an assistant correspondence clerk, salary and allowance, $1,200. That is a tremendous staff. Does the minister really think all that array is necessary for the work in the gold commissioner's office there ? He himself was there and looked into it. What I am told is that there is an aggregation of men there absolutely unnecessary. Any business man could do' the work with a very much less number of men and expense.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Of the names mentioned, Munroe, Macfarlane and Pepin are not in the employ there at all, and their places have not been filled. Macfarlane is employed as mining inspector on one of the creeks at Granville in the place of another man who has left the service. These are some of the decreases I mentioned.
Does the minister not think that the pruning knife could still be applied ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It looks to me as if it could. I did succeed in getting some pruning done. I have discussed the matter very fully with the present commissioner, and although he may not be as anxious to apply the pruning knife as my hon. friend, still I think lie will do what is right, and I hope the staff will not be allowed to remain over the requirements, if it is too large. It does look bulky for the amount of business.

The minister must take into consideration the fact that the commissioner lives night and day with these people, and the last thing in the world he wants to do is to recommend that any of them be cut down. If the minister waits until that is done, he w'ill wait a long time.
I think he ought to exercise his own judgment about that. If it was a large place, where the people were distributed a good deal, the commissioner would have all the more liberty that way, but they form a circle of their own, and it would be like cutting out one of his own family for the commissioner to make recommendations in that way. I hope he will do what is right, but I do not think there is much hope that he will face the live flesh with the idea that he is going to cut down their salaries and living allowance, because I do not think he is courageous enough to do it. As regards Mr. Congdon, the local adviser, he was for a long time the representative of the government as controller or administrator of estates ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is it true that, although the law required he should give bonds, he never did give security, all the time he was administrator of public estates ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not aware that he acted twice in that capacity, that is before he was commissioner and after he was commissioner.

Yes, he was in and out all the time.
Mr. OLIVER, I am not aware that he gave bonds on either occasion. I am satisfied that on one occasion he did not.
I think the papers will show that he never gave either an individual bond or a guarantee bond or anything of the kind. Who is administrator now ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Senkler, the present legal adviser, and administrator during the absence of Mr. Henderson.
Does he give bond ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He Is under a bond of

Is it also correct that Mr. Congdon, all the time he administered the estates as public administrator, never really made any statement with reference to any estate he administered, and that the department has not a single statement made by him of' a complete estate-of the transactions from start to finish.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am not able to answer definitely. I am under the impression however, that, so far as our department is concerned, my hon. friend is probably correct. However, I understand that the case Is that the administrator of estates-as the practice was there-was under the direction of the local government, the Yukon council. We appointed him and paid his salary, but, as I understand it, his administration was in accordance with the laws and ordinances of the Yukon council, and it was understood that his responsibilities were to them and not to us. For that reason, the statement that he would make would naturally be to the Yukon council, not to us.

Is it not true that the public administrator represented the Minister of the Interior ? If so, surely the minister here ought to have statements of his administration. It does not seem to me that the Bill is not filled when he is simply left to the tender mercies of the council which he himself dominates. Mr. Congdon is a rather dominatingly-inclined man, as shown by his whole history. He went out and went in a good many times, and never went back without having an increase in his salary, a very material increase. He was a kind of character who really controlled and had a dominating influence. He was commissioner some time, and member of the council generally. It would be an odd thing to have the public administrator accountable to himself as a member of the council. Is the minister aware whether he ever made a statement of an estate he managed as public administrator-finished statements and duly audited, before the local government ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, I am not aware how the business was transacted between himself and the local government in that connection. I may say that I have found the position as it was, and 1 stated it to my hon. friend, entirely unsatisfactory, for practically the reasons which he has placed before the House and because of the divided responsibility, so to speak. The responsibility was not definitely fixed, either with the Yukon council or with the government.

We, I assume, took it for granted, that the Yukon Council, having passed laws and ordinances under which the administration was to be carried on, would see to it that the laws and ordinances were properly administered. They, on the other hand, possibly thought that, as we appointed the administrator and paid him we were looking after the matter. I am afraid that, as a result of the examination made last summer by Mr. Beddoe-I think the report has been brought down-the matter was not in a condition that was satisfactory, or, I will go so far as to say, creditable to any of the parties concerned. I propose to cure that difficulty for the future. We did cure it in a measure when Mr. Senkler was appointed, by our requiring him to deposit securities to the amount of $10,000. There was a question raised as to our right to do that, the supposition being that it was the right or duty of the Yukon council to do it. However, we required the deposit of the security. And, in the Bill now before the House in regard to the Yukon, we propose to take the responsibility in regard to the administration of estates, to appoint the administrator, to require him to give security, and, while he administers the estates subject to the laws and ordinances of the Yukon council, he will make an accounting to the representative of the Auditor General. That will be more satisfactory. It is not that we wish to take from the rights or responsibilities of the local government, but we feel the condition in the past was such that we are warranted in future, in such an important and delicate matter, in absolutely fixing the responsibility. We will be quite prepared to fix the responsibility and place it entirely on the local government, but, if we are to assume any part of it, we "want to assume it all.

I am glad to hear the statement made by the minister. I assume that, under the new arrangement, we shall not have what appears to me to be such a scandal as has been there for so many years. There is one other question we ought to have satisfactorily at rest; Is it not the intention of the government to demand from Mr. Congdon an account of his stewardship ? He has been there, he has administered estates, he has acted as guardian for infants and had had charge of trust mattters dealing with the most intimate relations that the government has with its wards; and all the time he has been there, as we have seen, he has not really finished up an estate so far as putting in a statement that anybody could get hold of, properly audited and shown to be absolutely correct. Does not the minister think that Mr. Congdon should be called upon to make a full report of every eslate he has had in his charge, thoroughly

audited, and that the past negligence should be atoned for, at least by having it as far as can be effected, put in regular shape ?
I think that is the only thing that can he done to secure the government from the imputation of allowing its representative there to carry on matters of that kind in a very lax way. And I do not think it w ould be at all improper that Mr. Congdon should be asked to give a thorough and complete statement of every estate that he has managed and to have that statement thoroughly audited if it has not already been audited, and made as plain as it can be made at this late date.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I feel not at all in a pleasant position in this matter of administration of estates so far as we have been able to reach a statement in regard to them. There is, no doubt, something to be said in favour of the view taken by my hon. friend. The difficulty that might, or may, arise if we decide to take such action is that we may not have the right to call for the statement. The position may be taken that I have suggested-1 believe may very weH be taken-that the accounting is not to us but to the local government. It does not appear that there is any legislation or any definite delegation of authority that would put us in a position to absolutely demand this accounting.
May I ask the minister, is it not the fact that either the government here is in a position to demand that accounting or the government there is in that position ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Precisely.

Then, as the government here practically controls the government there by its appointed members, there is no difficulty in the government getting at the matter. I am not stating this to make a point against any one or anything of that kind; but I think it will be quite too bad- to say nothing stronger-that the matter should be left in the position in which it is. For instance, I have the right, I believe, to move for a return, showing the estates administered by the public administrator in the Yukon, and I suppose the House would pass a motion for a return of that kind and that we ought to have it. But that will not be necessary if the minister himself will see that, through their own legislation or through their control of the government of the Yukon, that statement shall be made. I do not know' that I ought to press the minister, because I suppose he has gone as far as he can under the circumstances. But as regards the present legal adviser, who is receiving the people's money as an employee of the government, is it proper for him to put himself at the head of a political organization, and fight out political campaigns, strike down opponents, boost up his 321
friends, with all the arts that he can use? The present incumbent of that office, Mr. Senlcler, is he disposed to take that line of conduct? If he does and I were in the Yukon, I would never let him rest. Mr. Congdon was legal adviser, he was commissioner, and almost everything by turns, always well paid for it, and all the time he wras an ardent partisan, continually menacing, threatening and cajoling in order to work up a party interest. It does not seem to me that men who are paid by the people's money and put in official positions, should be allowed to do that out there any more than they would be here. I cannot conceive that Mr. Senkler would be a man of that stamp.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not understand that the hon. gentleman suggests that Mr. Senkler is taking that course, I think it would be very far from his character. As for Mr. Congdon, I think it is fair to say that in my judgment the hon. gentleman has presented the case in a very extreme light. Mr. Congdon was legal adviser of the government in the Yukon, and on the retirement of the Hon. Mr. Ross from the commission-ership, Mr. Congdon was promoted to the commissionership. There may have been an interval during which he was not legal adviser or commissioner, but it was practically a promotion from the position of legal adviser to that of commissioner. I cannot agree that any slur is to be cast upon Mr. Congdon for partisan or political action while he was commissioner. It is true, he retired from the commissionership, and became a candidate as a supporter of the government. In the contest he was unsuccessful. There have been grave statements made as to the. methods in which the political contest was conducted which resulted in his defeat. I am not prepared to say whether those assertions are correct or not. But I have heard no such assertions in regard to his conduct when he was reappointed as legal adviser. When Mr. Mclnnes was commissioner I had no knowledge of any political activity on his part.
