He was acting as legal adviser amongst the people who had supported him for the position of member of parliament. True, he did not quarrel with those people. But I am bound to say that so far as my observation went while I was in the Yukon, he was not in any sense using his position as legal adviser to advance any one's political interest. He seemed to be attending strictly to the business he was appointed to do. I am bound to say that I know of no person whose qualifications are better than those of Mr. Congdon. Any one who knows him will agree that he is a very brilliant man, with a very good knowledge of law, and a most excellent method of expression. Besides, he is a man of absolutely blameless private life.
What is the reason for all these timber men?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We pay members of the mounted police who are stationed on the creeks, ten per cent on the collection of timber dues. We have one timber inspector, Charles Sylvester.

I find here that you have Mr. Martin, crown timber and land agent, $2,250 for nine months; you have W. H. Povah, clerk of timber and land office, $2,000 for nine months; you have Mr. Sugrue, timber inspector, $1,400 for nine months, and Mr. Sylvester, timber inspector, $1,800 for nine months. Those are in the timber branch. I do not think that the timber business is very heavy in the Yukon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Martin and Sugrue are not now in the employ of the government Povah is employed in the gold commissioner's office as stenographer. We have only one officer in the timber business; that is Mr. Sylvester.

Well, that makes it better. It would seem that the gold commissioner's office, the mining engineers and the inspectors might all work together. It is a cognate business. What does Mr. A. J. Beaudette, mining engineer, do?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I notice that the Yukon ' World and Official Gazette ' got $3,520, a large part of which was for printing and a part for advertising. Does the minister himself supervise that ? The Whitehorse ' Star,' for advertising the mining regulations for twelve months, got $600 and also something for advertising. These payments seem to be large. Then a lot of smaller papers, some of them in eastern Canada, received various sums. What are the reasons for running down here and publishing these advertisements?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We publish the mining regulations in the Dawson and Whitehorse papers and in some of the British Columbia papers pretty fully. We also publish in some of the leading eastern papers in centres like Montreal and Toronto a synopsis of our homestead and mining regulations and we charge the part of the advertisement relating to mining regulations to this Yukon vote. But that is only a small part of the expenditure.
Where are the insane taken charge of?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In the New Westminster insane asylum.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Beaudette is, in my estimation, the most valuable man we have in the Yukon. His duty is to satisfy the recorders or the gold commissioner, as the case may be, as to the facts upon the ground with regard to any matter of dispute that may arise.
And is necessary in that regard, I dare say.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Whereas the other mining recorders and inspectors are local officials who accept entries for mining claims and collect royalties and do other office duties, Mr. Beaudette is the man out on the creek who actually inspects the work.
Could the collections be made by the gold commissioner's clerks?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These are the collections made on the creeks.
I find that the Povahs seem to be quite a family up there. There are three of them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is only one of that family, Mr. W. F. Povah, who is now in the employ of the government. He is a stenographer and he was formerly in the timber office. The others are not in the service.
Is the grant for the local council of $125,000 given them in a lump sum?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
How is it audited?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a quarterly audit by the Auditor General. The accounts do not go to the Department of the Interior; they go direct to the Auditor General and are audited by him. Of course, there is a local accountant. The Auditor General is sending one of his officials to the Yukon now to make an audit on the ground. Under the Bill which is now before the House we propose that the accounts of the Yukon, both local and federal, shall be audited in the Yukon by a representative of the Auditor General ; that is to say, that the Auditor General shall officially be there for a part of the year to audit the accounts. Without waiting for this legislation the Auditor General has sent one of his men to make such an audit under the authority that he now possesses or believes himself to possess.

Well, according to Mr. Beddoe's report, it is not a bad thing to have it done.
